The libido drug women want is testosterone

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (647 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that these days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone.
  • Sources indicate that some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S.
  • Recent findings suggest that not many studies have looked at testosterone’s effects on libido in premenopausal women, but preliminary data in that area are also promising, according to a 2026 research review in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that Yih coauthored.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that these days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone. Interest is “coming from all directions,” says the University of California, Irvine Health urologist. A major source: women who hope testosterone can boost the female libido. Only about a decade ago, women looking for libido treatments had few medical options — even though women of all ages struggle with low sexual desire.

Sources indicate that some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has yet to approve a female testosterone product, despite years of research suggesting it can boost sexual function and desire among postmenopausal women. Female testosterone products are approved in countries including the United Kingdom and Australia.

Recent findings suggest that not many studies have looked at testosterone’s effects on libido in premenopausal women, but preliminary data in that area are also promising, according to a 2026 research review in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that Yih coauthored. “I have seen it change people’s lives,” Yih notes. The hormone seems to make the female brain more receptive to sexual stimuli; it also promotes physical effects that enhance sexual pleasure, such as increased blood flow to the genitals. Right now, American women interested in these potential benefits have to look for them off-label. But that may change. In September, the FDA held a public meeting on testosterone use among menopausal women, “with the goal of informing future research and potential drug development in this area,” says Kaveeta Vasisht, the FDA’s associate commissioner for women’s health.

Recent findings suggest that the hormone has a rocky regulatory past. In 2004, an FDA advisory panel unanimously voted against approving a testosterone patch for women, citing a lack of safety data. There are still outstanding questions on that front, Yih says—like how, if at all, long-term use affects risk of conditions such as breast cancer and heart disease. Then, in 2011, a pair of Phase III trials found that testosterone therapy didn’t significantly outperform a placebo — a benchmark the FDA looks for when deciding whether to approve a newly introduced drug. That’s not to say testosterone didn’t work, says Tami Rowen, an ob-gyn at UC San Francisco. Rather, it seemed that hype about the hormone was so strong that study participants went in with sky-high expectations, leading even the placebo group to report benefits. The treatment was a “victim of its own success,” Rowen says.

It has been revealed that interest hasn’t let up, though. By one estimate, the U.S. female prescription rate for all uses rose from 0.4 out of every 1,000 women in 2018, to 1.8 out of every 1,000 women in 2026. That’s an increase of nearly 400 percent. With so much buzz, the potential placebo effect remains “the biggest problem with testosterone right now,” Rowen notes.

Another outstanding question, Yih says, is whether using testosterone long-term increases the risk of breast cancer and heart disease.

According to recent reports, women seeking a libido boost do have non-hormonal options. In 2015, the FDA approved Addyi, the first treatment for low libido in premenopausal women. The drug seemingly raises levels of neurotransmitters that promote sexual desire while tamping down those that block it. A competitor, Vyleesi, hit shelves in 2019. Then, last year, regulators expanded Addyi’s use to postmenopausal women younger than 65. An international group of experts, including Rowen, issued recommendations for treating low female libido in 2025 in Sexual Medicine Reviews. Psychological therapies and Addyi are backed by the strongest evidence, the group found.

Recent findings suggest that rowen presently has her eye on in-development products including Lybrido. The drug, which is slated to enter a Phase III clinical trial in Europe, aims to rev sex drive in the brain and enhance physical arousal. The demand for new treatments is there, Rowen says. “Women deserve better than placebo.”.

NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson loses reelection in North Carolina

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (654 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson, right, here at a hearing in June, lost his reelection bid in North Carolina's 9th District.
  • Sources indicate that north Carolina Rep.
  • Hudson fell to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator who was leading  51 percent to 49 percent Thursday afternoon  when The Associated Press called the race in North Carolina’s 9th District.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson, right, here at a hearing in June, lost his reelection bid in North Carolina's 9th District. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Sources indicate that north Carolina Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee, has lost his race for reelection, a stinging defeat for the man charged with preserving the House majority for the GOP.

Hudson fell to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator who was leading  51 percent to 49 percent Thursday afternoon  when The Associated Press called the race in North Carolina’s 9th District.

Hudson had already conceded the race Wednesday, when it became clear that his path to victory was closing off.

It has been revealed that “[The] voters of North Carolina’s 9th District made their choice and I respect it,” he mentioned in a statement. “Since 2013 I’ve worked for North Carolina families. That includes the soldiers and families at Fort Bragg, who sacrifice more for this country than most people will ever know.”.

Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose his seat during a midterm election this decade. In 2022, Upcoming York Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney lost reelection while serving as chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

Recent findings suggest that republicans across North Carolina experienced devastating losses on election night. As of Thursday afternoon, Democrats had also flipped the seats of Reps. Addison McDowell, Brad Knott and Tim Moore, as well as the open seat of retiring Rep. Chuck Edwards. The races for five other GOP-held seats remain uncalled, while Democratic Rep. Don Davis was reelected despite being targeted for defeat under a upcoming GOP-drawn congressional map. Republicans also lost control of the North Carolina House and lost seats in the state Senate.

It has been revealed that north Carolina’s 9th District, which includes the Eastern Piedmont region and the Fayetteville area, was far from the House battlefield for much of the midterm cycle. President Donald Trump carried the seat by 16 points in 2024, according to calculations by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales, and Hudson won a seventh term the same year by nearly 19 points. Hudson also held a financial advantage over Ojeda, raising $4.2 million to Ojeda’s $2.9 million through mid-October.

But in the waning weeks of the campaign, signs of Republican concern grew and Hudson’s campaign began spending on ads.

In a recent development, ojeda was first elected to the West Virginia Senate in 2016. He ran for the U.S. House two years later as a Trump-voting Democrat but lost that race to Republican Carol Miller. He then briefly ran for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination and also challenged GOP Sen. Shelley Moore Capito later that cycle but lost in the Democratic primary.

Ojeda moved to North Carolina in 2020, he told CityView, a local magazine, and he revealed his challenge to Hudson last year.

According to recent reports, throughout the campaign, he attacked the incumbent over his support for Trump’s agenda, particularly the war in Iran. Ojeda is a retired Army major and the district is home to Fort Bragg, the nation’s largest Army base by population, where the Democrat was previously stationed for more than a decade.

Industry observers note that “We did the impossible,’’ Ojeda told supporters Tuesday night. “We took on the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, a man with political connections, the billionaire donors, and the entire Washington establishment standing beside him.”.

Hudson, 55, is finishing his seventh term in the House and his second term as NRCC chair. He had no primary opponent this year and had grown used to winning reelection by comfortable margins.

Sources indicate that as a legislator, Hudson focused much of his policy agenda on health concerns such as federal pandemic preparedness programs. He serves on the House Energy and Commerce Committee and chairs the panel's Communications and Technology Subcommittee.

This year’s El Niño is unlike any other on record

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (257 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it was an unprecedented year for El Niño, the weather-changing ocean pattern defined by warmer-than-normal surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific.
  • In September, the region’s daily average sea surface temperature reached the most extreme level ever recorded: more than 3.03 degrees Celsius above the 30-year average (dashed line).
  • It has been revealed that all that hot water has fueled the most active Pacific hurricane season on record.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it was an unprecedented year for El Niño, the weather-changing ocean pattern defined by warmer-than-normal surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. By October 18, the ocean area that researchers use to monitor El Niño’s severity climbed to an average temperature of over 30° Celsius (86° Fahrenheit) for the first time in history. From there, it kept on rising.

In September, the region’s daily average sea surface temperature reached the most extreme level ever recorded: more than 3.03 degrees Celsius above the 30-year average (dashed line). The World Meteorological Organization predicts that sea surface temperatures may peak at 3.7 degrees above that average by January. The two previous strongest El Niños on record emerged in 1997 and 2015.

It has been revealed that all that hot water has fueled the most active Pacific hurricane season on record. By mid-October, 331 units of cyclone energy had accumulated, beating out 2018’s record of 318 units. It has also unleashed heat into the atmosphere, affecting distant circulation patterns and leading to an extraordinarily quiet Atlantic hurricane season.

Recent findings suggest that 2026’s El Niño will be felt well beyond the Latest Year. Precipitation and drought impacts are expected across the world through spring 2027. And the global heating effect could compound with human-caused climate warming to make 2027 the hottest year ever recorded.

The heat that El Niño unleashes into the atmosphere shifts storm tracks and weather patterns globally. Here are some of the most significant observed and anticipated effects.

#31229. At the Races: After the deluge

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2126 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

At the Races: After the deluge

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tuesday’s rout by Democrats has led one group dedicated to electing more Republican women to Congress to warn of a “crisis-level decline” of female GOP members on Capitol Hill.
  • Danielle Barrow, the president of Women for Women Action Fund, drew parallels between this week’s results and the 2018 blue wave.
  • “After 2018, when Republicans lost 40 seats and elected only one new Republican woman, the party made a real commitment to recruiting and investing in women – and it worked,” Barrow said in a statement Wednesday, adding that women accounted for 11 of the 15 House seats the GOP picked up in the 2020 election.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tuesday’s rout by Democrats has led one group dedicated to electing more Republican women to Congress to warn of a “crisis-level decline” of female GOP members on Capitol Hill.

Danielle Barrow, the president of Women for Women Action Fund, drew parallels between this week’s results and the 2018 blue wave.

“After 2018, when Republicans lost 40 seats and elected only one new Republican woman, the party made a real commitment to recruiting and investing in women – and it worked,” Barrow said in a statement Wednesday, adding that women accounted for 11 of the 15 House seats the GOP picked up in the 2020 election. But she cautioned that the party needs to sustain that focus across election cycles.

Sources indicate that “Republicans cannot only make this investment after a wipeout election and abandon it when things improve,” she noted. “It is time for party leaders to treat this as a permanent strategy, not a crisis response.”.

In a recent development, the ranks of House Republican women won’t plummet to as low as after the 2018 elections, when the caucus had just 13 female members. At least 18 Republican women have won House races so far, according to The Associated Press, and two others are leading as of Thursday afternoon. The conference is likely to see two new female members: Florida’s Sydney Gruters, the wife of RNC Chairman Joe Gruters, and Washington state’s Amanda McKinney, who holds a comfortable lead as votes continue to be counted.

Still, those figures are worlds apart from House Democrats, whose caucus will have more than 100 women next year.

“We have always known that when women run, women win,” Florida Rep. Lois Frankel, chair of the member-led Elect Democratic Women PAC, noted in a statement Wednesday.

Those incoming fresh members span the ideological range of the party, including progressives from New York and California who scored big primary wins this summer, to more moderate Democrats who flipped seats in Virginia and Pennsylvania.

House Democrats had set a public goal this cycle to push their female membership past 100. Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who is retiring at the end of the year, said electing Democratic women had been her “passion” since she joined the House in 1987.

“We made a decision to make more room for women at the tables of power – and generations of candidates, organizers and supporters have carried that work forward,” she stated.

Blue breakthrough: Democrats flipped the House and Senate this week, giving the party one of its biggest nights in decades. On the Senate side, they wrested seats from Republicans in Texas, South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and Ohio, while finally flipping Maine. Meanwhile, on the House side, Democrats were on track to not just win every race rated a Toss-up by Inside Elections but also pick up seats in deep-red territory that weren’t considered competitive until late in the cycle. Mary Ellen and Daniela summed up their initial election night takeaways, including how Democratic moderates and progressives both cheered the results and why many of Trump’s picks flopped at the ballot box.

Not going anywhere: The top Senate Democrat, Charles E. Schumer of New York, is confident he will be elected majority leader by his caucus, especially after the party’s resounding midterm wins. Several of his incoming members have promised to support others, our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports, but the reality is there’s no real plausible alternative. Schumer’s own seat is up in 2028.

Redistricting rout: Republicans’ redistricting gambit hasn’t paid off as they’d hoped, the latest election results show, with the GOP appearing poised to flip only a handful of redrawn seats. Democratic incumbents who sought reelection from their reconfigured seats appeared poised to all win, although the race for Rep. Darren Soto’s Central Florida seat remained uncalled as of Thursday afternoon.

It has been revealed that taking the chair: Among the bruising defeats that North Carolina Republicans suffered this week was National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson’s loss to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator. Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose reelection this decade after Upcoming York’s Sean Patrick Maloney , who lost in 2022 while serving as the DCCC chair.

New senators: The incoming Senate Democratic class includes a returning senator, a former governor, two lieutenant governors and a congressman, a notable amount of governing experience. Meanwhile, five Republican House members are moving across the Rotunda after winning open Senate seats.

Member-to-governor pipeline grows: Five newly elected governors will be departing Capitol Hill to become the top executive of their state or territory, Savannah reports. Additionally, two former members who also served in the Biden administration were elected governor, though a trio of House Republicans fell short in their gubernatorial bids.

Comeback season: Roll Call’s Nick Eskow reports on the former members who are poised to return to the House or Senate next year, with at least seven winning comeback bids Tuesday.

In a recent development, the firsts: Several candidates made history this week with their elections to Congress or the governorships of their state. Roll Call’s Andrew Menezes rounds up the milestone wins.

D.C. in the House: Robert White, D.C.’s newly elected nonvoting delegate, told our colleague Nina Heller that he prepares to lobby fellow Democrats next year to support D.C. statehood. A potential selling point: The party could tackle affordability concerns better with two Democratic senators from the deep-blue District, he mentioned.

Keeping count: As of 4:30 p.m. Thursday, Democrats had flipped 42 seats in the House and seven in the Senate, according to the AP. Republicans have so far picked up two House seats, both through redistricting. Twenty-eight House contests and two Senate races (Alaska and Mississippi) remain uncalled as of publication time. Check out Roll Call’s results tracker for updates as the races are called.

Indie losses: Independent Senate hopefuls running in deep-red states did not find success on Tuesday, even in races without a Democrat on the ballot. In Nebraska, former union leader Dan Osborn came up short in his second Senate bid. In Idaho, former state legislator Todd Achilles failed to dislodge Sen. Jim Risch, while Navy veteran Brian Bengs couldn’t topple South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds. In Montana, where the Democratic nominee did not drop out, former university president Seth Bodnar lost to Republican Kurt Alme. On the House side, Alaska GOP Rep. Nick Begich comfortably leads commercial fisherman Bill Hill, though below the 50 percent threshold needed to avoid a ranked-choice runoff. With votes still being counted, the AP had yet to call the race at publication time.

According to recent reports, not just Congress: The blue wave that broke Republican majorities on Capitol Hill also washed over state legislatures. Democrats are poised to hold newly introduced majorities in 12 legislative chambers, including the North Carolina House and Texas House, according to the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, although some results aren’t official yet. The party also won governing trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Meanwhile, in blue states, Democrats tightened their grip on government: In Rhode Island, Republicans are on track to hold just 10 seats in the entire 113-member legislature, while next door in Connecticut, the 36-seat Senate could have as few as three GOP members.

Sources indicate that blame game: As Republicans take stock of what went wrong for them in the midterms, Vice President JD Vance was quick to point to the Iran conflict as an insurmountable albatross. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance said in a lengthy X post. “If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. … But everyone knows why we lost.”.

But the tariffs: A pair of Republican former senators, Arizona’s Jeff Flake and Pennsylvania’s Patrick J. Toomey, both also urged their party to focus on the impact of Trump’s tariff policies. “Arbitrary and capricious tariffs directly raised costs for all American consumers,” Toomey wrote Wednesday on X. “Many voted for Democrats yesterday.”.

Staying put: Pennsylvania Rep. Brendan F. Boyle indicates he will remain in the House, where he’s poised to become the next Budget Committee chair, rather than launch a Democratic primary challenge to Sen. John Fetterman next cycle.

It has been revealed that bayh Bayh Bayh: A third generation of Indiana’s famed Bayh family won political office this week, with Beau Bayh’s election as secretary of state. Bayh, a Marine Corps veteran, follows in the footsteps of his father, Evan Bayh, who won the same post 40 years ago before going on to serve as governor and senator, and his late grandfather, Birch Bayh, who won three terms in the Senate. Indiana Democrats had a breakthrough election this week, defeating GOP Rep. Victoria Spartz, winning a second statewide office, unseating the speaker and breaking the GOP supermajority in the state House.

A win and a loss: Nebraska Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts won reelection, but his wife, Democrat Susanne Shore, lost a special election for a seat on University of Nebraska Board of Regents, which governs the university system. Shore, who lost to a fellow Democrat in the officially nonpartisan race, was making her first bid for elective office.

In a recent development, bans on the ballot: Voters in Arizona, Nebraska and Washington state have approved newly introduced measures barring transgender athletes from participating in girls sports. A similar proposal in Colorado also appears likely to pass, although the AP had yet to call it as of publication time.

Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections shares 15 initial lessons from the midterm elections, from the president’s “political mortality” to candidate quality and the power of personal brands. And, Nathan writes, as bad a night as it was for Republicans, it could have been even worse.

Industry observers note that as Maine goes: The Newly introduced York Times caught up with with Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her bid for a sixth term in Maine. Collins, who had survived tough cycles before, spoke of getting “caught up in the Trump tsunami” and how she finally had her “Margaret Chase Smith moment.”.

Industry observers note that “These are extinction-level numbers”: Texas Monthly sat down for an interview with former state House Speaker Dade Phelan, who anticipated a down-ballot GOP rout but not the full extent of it. “MAGA needs to be dead,’’ noted the Republican, who led the push to impeach state Attorney General Ken Paxton in 2023 and then was targeted for defeat by Trump. He opted against reelection this year.

Corruption a top concern: The Associated Press reported that its 2026 voter poll found corruption at the top of the list of concerns for voters who helped sweep Democrats into power on Capitol Hill.

Tar Heeled: Among the states where Republicans suffered their biggest defeats Tuesday, perhaps none was more stunning than North Carolina, where they've so far lost five U.S. House seats and are trailing in one another and lost control of the state House. The (Raleigh) News & Observer looks at how maps “designed to deliver strong Republican majorities [failed] so spectacularly at that goal.”.

Support and discord: Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s sharply critical views toward Israel roiled the Jewish community in Michigan. But exit polling suggests most Jewish voters backed him, albeit in smaller numbers than they might have had a different Democrat run, Religion News Service reports.

In a recent development, that's how many House districts won by Trump in 2024 have been called for Democratic candidates by the AP as of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time on Thursday.

Twenty-eight additional Trump-won districts remain uncalled at publication time, and Democrats are presently leading in eight of those races.

The figures stand in sharp contrast to the start of the cycle, when there were just 13 House Democrats in districts that backed Trump in 2024.

Since then, several Republican-led states redrew their congressional maps in an effort to increase the number of Trump-won districts and improve their party’s chances of holding the House.

In large part, this effort appears to have backfired in 2026, with the Democratic wave cresting high enough to wash over dozens of Trump-won districts. Twenty-one of the 52 Democratic wins so far have come in states that redrew their congressional lines: Texas (six Trump-won seats), North Carolina (six), Ohio (five), Florida (three) and Alabama (one).

Congressional Republicans are holding leadership elections next week as they transition from the majority to the minority party. Speaker Mike Johnson is not seeking his conference’s top post, setting up a clash to be the next House minority leader. On the Senate side, South Dakota’s John Thune hopes to continue leading his party in the chamber.

As Democrats look to next era, the veto and the filibuster await

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1498 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, senate Minority Leader Charles E.
  • As Democrats continue their victory lap after their massive wins on election night, outside groups and incoming freshmen are already turning up the pressure — and laying out competing visions of what the next two years should look like.
  • It has been revealed that for Senate Democratic leader Charles E.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer greets House Minority Whip Katherine Clark at the Center for American Progress Action Fund’s “Results to Roadmap” event on Thursday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

As Democrats continue their victory lap after their massive wins on election night, outside groups and incoming freshmen are already turning up the pressure — and laying out competing visions of what the next two years should look like.

It has been revealed that for Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, it bears repeating that “the Democrats aren’t all exactly the same.”.

“The most vital lesson of this whole election, and one we all need to internalize if we’re going to truly build a durable majority, is populism and moderation are not mutually exclusive,” he mentioned at a Center for American Progress Action Fund event on Thursday.

Voters are expecting results as Democrats claim a mandate to address costs and corruption. “Our majority will be measured against one test and one test only: Have we made your life better?” Schumer said.

He acknowledged, however, that their plans could run into a President Donald Trump-sized wall: the presidential veto.

In a recent development, “Will everything pass? Will Trump sign all of it into law? Knowing Trump’s and Republicans’  intransigence, of course not. But I will promise the American people: The Democratic Party will fight to make your life more affordable, your government more competent, your capital less corrupt, bill by bill, brick by brick, for as long as it takes for you to feel the difference,” Schumer said, hinting the road could be a long one.

But several progressive lawmakers and groups say the next Congress cannot be business as usual.

Indivisible, a progressive political organization that has described the Trump administration as a “fascistic clown show,” sent a memo to Senate Democratic offices Thursday morning urging them not to “squander” their momentum and to “fight at a level that matches the public’s demand for action.”.

“Who leads the party in this era must be an open question, not a coronation. It’s time to define what the next era of the Democratic Party will be,” the memo reads.

The group has been encouraging voters to speak up and demand their senators hold “a contested leadership election, not a cleared field for Schumer.”.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, Schumer has projected confidence he will keep his spot atop the caucus, especially after he helped pave the way for Tuesday’s blue wave. “I’ll be reelected as majority leader,” he said Wednesday. But the pressure campaign points to some tough math and harsh realities for the top Democrat — including some that mirror the woes of the outgoing Republican Majority Leader John Thune.

Among the demands outlined by Indivisible is one with a troubled recent history: “Breaking the filibuster on the first day of the latest session.”.

Democrats need to leverage “every procedural tool” if they “want the public to believe their campaign promises weren’t just more talk from politicians who are just like the old politicians they hated,” the memo reads.

In a recent development, the group isn’t alone in floating a new approach to the chamber’s 60-vote threshold for invoking cloture and ending debate. Some current and incoming lawmakers have signaled they would be open to going “nuclear” and abolishing the legislative filibuster, following in the footsteps of past majorities in both parties who have similarly changed how other Senate business is handled, like judicial nominees.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., argued in an op-ed in Time this week that Democrats could in some cases use existing tools, like a party-line process known as budget reconciliation, to pass their priorities. For non-budget items, like “bills to ban stock trading by federal officials or crack down on Trump’s corruption in plain sight,” Democrats should start by putting them up for a vote on the floor and letting “Republicans decide if they want to stay tied to such corruption.”.

“And, if they do, then let’s clear away Senate filibuster rules and pass the laws anyway,” she wrote.

Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas told NBC News on Monday ahead of his victory, “I believe the majority has the right to govern in this country, and the filibuster, which is not in the Constitution and is a Jim Crow relic, is leading to gridlock in our nation’s capital.”.

Schumer ignored a question about nuking the filibuster at Wednesday’s event, saying instead, “The first thing we’ll do is reduce costs and work the legislative process.”.

According to recent reports, it would take 51 votes in the Senate for Democrats to go “nuclear” and establish a newly introduced precedent, a math problem that Thune knows all too well. The Republican from South Dakota faced loud criticism from conservatives online and hard-liners in his own party who noted he wasn’t doing enough to try to pass a sprawling voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act. But Thune repeatedly insisted he didn’t have the votes to change the chamber’s filibuster rules.

Many senators fear that blowing up the 60-vote threshold would fundamentally change the role of the Senate and its ability to tap the brakes on legislation that doesn’t have durable bipartisan support. Democrats went through a similar debate over the filibuster in 2022, during Schumer's first stint as majority leader. Even as others in their party pushed to pass sweeping voting rights legislation by any means necessary, Kyrsten Sinema and Joe Manchin, then moderate Democratic senators, held firm against filibuster changes.

Sources indicate that and Schumer will have at least one Democrat on his hands who has already spoken up in defense of the filibuster, reversing his previous position. “I now recognize how key the filibuster is and the state our country would be in without it,” Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania wrote in a Washington Post op-ed earlier this summer, praising Sinema and Manchin as “courageous” holdouts who were wrongly “vilified” for holding the line.

Industry observers note that none of that points to an easy ride for the incoming Democratic majority leader. And if fights over the filibuster weren’t enough, the caucus is also bracing for a different kind of intraparty angst, this time over impeachment.

The next likely House Judiciary Committee chairman, Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., told reporters on Thursday: “I have not had a single member of Congress or even a candidate say we’ve got to start out by impeaching Donald Trump.”.

“For us, impeachment is not a fetish. It’s certainly not a taboo. We’ve impeached the guy twice,” he noted, referring to Democrats’ efforts during the first Trump administration. “The problem has been over on the Senate side, and for us, it is a tool in the constitutional toolkit.”.

Even if the House were to impeach Trump, a conviction would require a two-thirds supermajority vote in the Senate. And some Democrats are eager not to waste their hard-earned political capital on an impeachment quest that could alienate moderate voters and do nothing to bring down costs for everyday Americans.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who boosted candidates in battleground races and recently released a roadmap for the fresh Congress, remarked at the CAP event on Thursday that lawmakers should “hold oversight hearings and expose the corruption of this administration. I’m not suggesting that that necessarily leads to impeachment. Maybe it does.”.

Sounding more certain for Democrats in both chambers is their desire to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran.

But that could be dealt with in the lame duck if Rep. Thomas Massie’s, R-Ky., resolution prevails next week. His proposal includes eight articles of impeachment, including allegations that Hegseth violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

In a recent development, hegseth stated in a video on Thursday of impeaching: “Didn’t work against President Trump. Won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”.

Indivisible’s memo names impeaching Hegseth as a priority, as well as blocking a “business-as-usual” National Defense Authorization Act in the lame duck and refusing to fund the Department of Defense if “it doesn’t cut off money for the war.”.

But it’s not clear that Democrats in Congress are ready to play that kind of hard ball. As they weigh their approach to the next era, they’re still half-stunned themselves by their larger than expected wins — and trying to put themselves in the best position ahead of the next elections in 2028.

It has been revealed that GOP Rep. Christopher H. Smith of Upcoming Jersey told reporters on Thursday at the Capitol he hopes Democrats don’t hold up the NDAA “for the good of the country.”.

It has been revealed that “The NDAA is such an important bill for our national security, and it’s usually very bipartisan. I hope it is,” he mentioned.

John Donnelly and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

  • Meeks, D-N.Y., the presumed next chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, plans to bring resolutions to the floor to “immediately” end the war with Iran when Democrats take control of the House in January, he wrote in a letter Thursday seeking his colleagues’ support to become chairman.
  • The letter, which officially confirmed his bid for the chairmanship, lays out his oversight agenda for the committee, which will also see considerable turnover on the GOP side of the dais.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and staffers cheer as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., takes the stage during a election night watch party in Washington on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Recent findings suggest that rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., the presumed next chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, plans to bring resolutions to the floor to “immediately” end the war with Iran when Democrats take control of the House in January, he wrote in a letter Thursday seeking his colleagues’ support to become chairman.

The letter, which officially confirmed his bid for the chairmanship, lays out his oversight agenda for the committee, which will also see considerable turnover on the GOP side of the dais.

Meeks and other Democrats have repeatedly forced votes this year on war powers resolutions seeking to end the Iran war, with a Meeks-sponsored one clearing both chambers of Congress.

But those resolutions have been nonbinding concurrent resolutions, since the 1973 War Powers Resolution only lays out a fast-track procedure the minority party can wield for concurrent resolutions in the House.

With a House majority, though, Democrats could bring binding joint resolutions to the floor.

Sources indicate that beyond war powers votes, Meeks also promised public hearings on the war. He also vowed hearings on a range of topics including the administration’s Venezuela policy and “repeated defiance of Congress's constitutional authority over war powers and trade.”.

“As chairman in the 120th Congress, oversight of this administration’s lawlessness and corruption will be at the top of the agenda,” Meeks wrote. “I will continue to advance a principled foreign policy grounded in our values, including support for Ukraine against Russian aggression.”.

In addition to Iran measures, Meeks also promised legislation focused on “clawing back Congress’s proper role in the making of American foreign policy” and a State Department reauthorization bill that puts guardrails on the administration and protects career diplomats.

Meanwhile, the GOP side of the committee is poised to lose at least a dozen lawmakers — or about half of its members — next year between retirements and election losses.

The departures include longtime members such as former Chairman Michael McCaul, R-Texas, who opted not to seek reelection, and Rep. Scott Perry, R-Pa., the Freedom Caucus chair who lost his reelection race.

According to recent reports, several other Republican committee members remained locked in races that were still too close to call as of Thursday afternoon, according to The Associated Press, potentially gutting the GOP committee bench further. They include GOP Rep. Young Kim of California, the East Asia and Pacific Subcommittee chair who was trailing her in race against fellow California Republican Rep. Ken Calvert.

Sources indicate that rep. Christopher H. Smith, R-N.J., who chairs the Africa Subcommittee, lamented the turnover Thursday but predicted a lot of interest among remaining House Republicans to fill the void.

Industry observers note that “There will be many who will want to be on it,” Smith told reporters. “We lost some really great people. Yesterday I can't tell you how sad I was about friends who are now not coming back.”.

Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

Latest Update: Scientists Studied Thousands of Ancient Skeletons and Found a Strange Truth About Human Progress

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (777 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It does a body good” slogan has some historical backing, at least in Europe.
  • It has been revealed that “When children and adolescents have access to sufficient, high-quality food, they grow taller, within the constraints of genetic factors,” Manon Stephan, an economic historian at Germany’s University of Tübingen, stated in a statement.
  • According to recent reports, to test that idea, Stephan and colleagues at Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology examined 18,457 bones from 783 sites in 45 countries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The dairy industry’s “Milk. It does a body good” slogan has some historical backing, at least in Europe. That’s one of the more surprising takeaways from a large study that used ancient skeletons to track how well people lived across Europe and Asia over the past 7,000 years. The researchers based their analysis on one telling measurement: human height.

It has been revealed that “When children and adolescents have access to sufficient, high-quality food, they grow taller, within the constraints of genetic factors,” Manon Stephan, an economic historian at Germany’s University of Tübingen, stated in a statement. “Therefore, height enables us to draw conclusions about living standards.”.

According to recent reports, to test that idea, Stephan and colleagues at Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology examined 18,457 bones from 783 sites in 45 countries. In the study, published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the team estimated people’s heights from their long bones. They then tracked how average height changed in each region and compared those changes with shifts in population density and technology.

It has been revealed that in China, men were taller 7,000 years ago, averaging 5 feet 10 inches. Over time, however, their height steadily declined, reaching a low of just 5 feet 3 inches on average in the 19th century. Chinese women’s height also declined, though less drastically, falling from an average of 5 feet 2 inches 7,000 years ago to 4 feet 10 inches in more recent times.

Recent findings suggest that trends like these would be nearly impossible to trace through written records alone. “In many parts of the world, any written sources that would allow us to draw conclusions about economic development appear quite late on our timeline and are patchy in their distribution,” Stephan mentioned. “That’s why we rely on bones.” The bones in question came from 22 Asian and 23 European countries and were taken from the graves of commoners in both densely populated and rural regions.

In Europe, by contrast, the trends went in a different direction. Around 5,000 years ago, men in northern Europe averaged just 5 feet 4 inches. However, the study authors wrote, as pastoralist peoples migrated from the steppes of Eastern Europe and western Siberia, they brought with them more advanced dairy farming and the genetic trait of lactose tolerance. This led to greater consumption of dairy products, which the study identifies as a leading factor in increased height. Average heights in northern Europe continued to climb into the early Middle Ages, but sometime between 500 and 1000 C.E., they began to decline, a trend that lasted until the end of the 19th century.

Women’s heights followed a similar pattern. China and Japan experienced the steepest declines, while Europe saw a rise, though a less steep one than among men.

The authors wrote that “human stature is a valuable indicator of nutritional status and health.” Reconstructing this indicator offers insight into which societies provided better health and nutrition to their people. Surprisingly, technological progress did not prove to be a major factor in improving either.

It has been revealed that “Our study also confirmed that technological progress does not automatically lead to greater height,” mentioned Jörg Baten, a professor of economic history at the University of Tübingen. “In China, for example, latest, higher-yielding rice varieties and other innovations were introduced in the 11th century [C.E.]. While the higher yields enabled the empire to remain the dominant power, they did not subsequently lead to a better standard of living for the general population. Instead, population density increased: People had more children because this was seen as a form of security in old age. This meant, however, that each individual had not more to eat, but less. And importantly the quality declined, for example, in terms of high-quality protein.”.

Industry observers note that europe’s findings on technology mirrored Asia’s. Improved technology helped support denser populations, but it didn’t increase average height or necessarily improve the nutritional value of food.

In a recent development, going forward, the authors hope to link more of these changes in height to shifts in social conditions or developments in agriculture. “This requires further research,” noted Mark Hudson, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology. “However, the statistical data reveal trends and provide clues as to when these changes occurred.”.

In a recent development, tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

How 4 states voted on election-related ballot measures

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Maryland voters fill out ballots at a polling site in Bowie on Tuesday.
  • More than 100 statewide ballot measures went before voters this week, including a handful that could shape future elections in their states.
  • Here’s a look at how those measures fared, including one in Alaska that hasn’t been called as yet:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Maryland voters fill out ballots at a polling site in Bowie on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

More than 100 statewide ballot measures went before voters this week, including a handful that could shape future elections in their states.

Here’s a look at how those measures fared, including one in Alaska that hasn’t been called as yet:.

Voters in Maryland on Tuesday approved an amendment to the state’s constitution that will make it easier for the state’s Democrat-controlled legislature to redraw the congressional map for the 2028 elections.

In a recent development, the outcome was a victory for Democrats, who could potentially eliminate the state’s lone Republican-held seat – the 1st District on Maryland’s Eastern Shore, represented by Rep. Andy Harris, the chair of the hard-line conservative House Freedom Caucus.

The Old Line State emerged as a bright spot in Democrats’ initiative to counter the redistricting wars initiated by President Donald Trump and turbocharged by the spring Supreme Court ruling that diluted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act and set off a slew of Republican-led map-remaking across the South.

But those GOP-led efforts appeared to backfire this week, with Democrats holding many of the redrawn seats in states such as Texas, Florida, Alabama and North Carolina.

Sources indicate that still, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore told reporters Wednesday that he was “ready to engage” with the legislature on a latest map, citing the threat of further redistricting in Republican states.

“Donald Trump is not done. He has already been very clear about his intention to go after additional states, to go after places like Mississippi and South Carolina and Indiana,” Moore remarked, according to video posted by WBAL-TV 11 News.

Following an unsuccessful attempt to redraw the Maryland map in February, Moore called a special August legislative session during which state lawmakers voted to put the redistricting amendment, known as Question 3, on the November ballot.

Recent findings suggest that the move faced immediate legal challenges from Republicans. Two Maryland courts ruled to block the measure from appearing on the ballot, finding that lawmakers had missed the legally imposed deadline to refer the ballot measure. The state’s Supreme Court, though, allowed the redistricting amendment to go before the voters, with changes to the ballot text.

State and national Democrats campaigned heavily for Question 3 as some public polling pointed to skepticism among voters. Former President Barack Obama even appeared in an ad urging voters to approve it.

Voters in the Show-Me State overwhelmingly rejected a Republican-drawn congressional map that sought to dismantle a safely Democratic seat in the Kansas City area.

Missouri Republicans enacted the upcoming lines in 2025, aiming to give them an advantage in seven of the state’s eight House districts, including the 5th District held by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver II.

A protracted legal and political tussle over the map ensued.

Sources indicate that the group People Not Politicians Missouri started a citizen petition to put the adoption of the map to a statewide vote. While the petition effort was pending, the state held its August primaries under the new lines. But in September, the state Supreme Court ruled that the 2025 map could not be used in the general election because of the pending ballot measure and ordered state officials to hold November’s election under the previous boundaries, first enacted in 2022.

According to recent reports, attempts to challenge the ruling in federal court ultimately proved unsuccessful, with the U.S. Supreme Court issuing an order that reinstated the 2022 map.

In a recent development, groups on both sides of the ballot measure, known as Proposition A, reportedly spent millions to persuade voters. But St. Louis Public Radio reported last week that while opponents of the 2025 map were actively campaigning against it, organized efforts in favor of Proposition A appeared “nearly nonexistent.”.

Republican efforts to try again and enact a latest congressional map for 2028 could be complicated by a constitutional amendment, approved by voters Tuesday, that curtails the power of state legislators to override the result of a voter-approved initiative.

Voters in Massachusetts opted this week not to join states such as California and Washington and adopt a nonpartisan primary system.

The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, would have replaced the state’s partisan primaries with an open primary under which all candidates would appear on the same ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to the general election.

Industry observers note that the outcome was a victory for the chorus of labor unions and progressive groups, including the Working Families Party, that opposed the measure. Holding so-called jungle primaries, the groups argued, could make it harder for candidates without financial resources or high name recognition to run for office.

It has been revealed that A bipartisan coalition that included the NAACP of Latest England and Republican former Gov. Charlie Baker supported the measure, arguing that open primaries would give voters more choice and create more competitive elections in a state dominated by Democrats.

Alaskans weighed in this year for the second time as many cycles on a ballot measure to revert to partisan primaries and repeal the state's top-four ranked choice voting system.

Sources indicate that with over 70 percent of the vote in, The Associated Press had yet to call the ballot initiative, known as Measure 2, which would also roll back certain campaign finance disclosure requirements. As of Thursday evening, the “no” side, which supports keeping the current election system, was narrowly ahead. The state has until Nov. 18 to finish counting outstanding ballots.

Recent findings suggest that under Alaska’s voting system, all candidates run on the same ballot during the primary. Then the top four candidates, regardless of party, advance to the general election, which is decided by ranked choice voting if no one takes a majority of the vote.

In 2024, Alaska voters narrowly voted to keep the current system in place.

National Republicans, though, have largely opposed ranked choice voting, including Trump, who has characterized Alaska’s voting system as a “scam.”.

It has been revealed that the state’s use of open primaries and the top-four ranked choice system has drawn fresh scrutiny this year. Outside groups spent substantial sums trying to boost underdog candidates during the Senate primary in an effort to hurt the front-runners. And several candidates in the Senate, House and governor’s races dropped out before the deadline to finalize the general election ballot, again trying to prevent splitting votes with their party front-runners.

Then last week, the Senate race was upended by a New York Times investigation that revealed operatives aligned with the Senate campaign of Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola helped recruit a candidate with a similar name to GOP incumbent Dan Sullivan in an attempt to stack the ballot with two Republicans with the same first and last names. The revelations have fueled an ongoing debate in the state about whether ranked choice voting encourages this kind of alleged campaign chicanery.

“We would not be having this conversation at all if we didn’t have a thing in place called ranked choice voting,” Mike Dunleavy, Alaska's outgoing Republican governor, told Fox News last week.

Industry observers note that dunleavy has ordered an investigation into the revelations, as has the Justice Department. The DOJ also sought to block the certification of the Senate result if the incumbent Sullivan loses. Last weekend, a federal court dismissed the lawsuit.

Alaska and Maine are the only two states that at the moment use ranked choice voting in regular federal elections, along with the District of Columbia.

Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • "We cannot afford to rely on outdated systems to oversee an increasingly complex financial sector," stated Rep.
  • A leading Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee introduced legislation Thursday aimed at helping regulators use technology to better spot financial stress turbocharged by artificial intelligence and around-the-clock payment systems.
  • Industry observers note that the draft bill, from Rep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"We cannot afford to rely on outdated systems to oversee an increasingly complex financial sector," stated Rep. Bill Foster, D-Ill., (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

A leading Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee introduced legislation Thursday aimed at helping regulators use technology to better spot financial stress turbocharged by artificial intelligence and around-the-clock payment systems.

Industry observers note that the draft bill, from Rep. Bill Foster, D-Ill., would require the Federal Reserve to work with other regulators to develop, test and publicly release model software that would improve the ability to assess market conditions in real time and respond promptly to cybersecurity and other threats.

The bill is designed to help regulators keep pace with new risks "driven largely by the development of state-of-the-art AI models," according to a summary.

The legislation is intended to help regulators provide financing to banks during crises and wind down failing banks. The model software would reduce the amount of manual compliance work that smaller financial institutions would have to do by providing standard data formats for regulatory reporting and tools to manage and transmit the information to regulators, according to a Foster spokesperson.

Industry observers note that “With advances in AI creating newly introduced cybersecurity threats and financial risks, it's more important than ever that we modernize the way we monitor the health of our financial institutions,” Foster stated in a statement. “We cannot afford to rely on outdated systems to oversee an increasingly complex financial sector.”.

Foster, who has a Ph.D. in physics and has been a leader on AI issues on the Financial Services panel, is in line to become chair of the Financial Institutions Subcommittee next year.

He has been mulling a challenge to ranking member Maxine Waters, D-Calif., to chair the full committee in the new Congress. But Foster is now “leaning toward not running,” a person familiar with his thinking remarked.

Sources indicate that waters already has a confirmed challenger in Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., who on Thursday circulated a "Dear Colleague" letter seeking the support of House Democrats for his bid.

Casten touted his “career at the intersection of business, science and public policy." Before entering Congress, he worked in clean energy and co-founded a organization that converted industrial waste energy into usable power.

In his letter, Casten cited the need to lower housing and insurance costs, protect consumers from fraud, address risks posed by cryptocurrency and prediction markets and guard against the next financial crisis. He also promised to hold the Trump administration accountable for ethical lapses.

He's got a tough road ahead of him, however. Every Financial Services Democrat except Casten, Foster and Rep. Sam Liccardo of California signed an Oct. 21 letter to House Democrats in support of Waters. That show of support came after Casten made it known he was interested and it was clear that Foster had been considering his own bid.

Although Foster may not compete for the chairmanship, he has recently talked to Waters about changing how the committee operates.

“He wants a variety of members to play a role in legislation brought up in committee,” the source familiar with his thinking said. He’s also seeking more input on witnesses who testify at subcommittee hearings.

Industry observers note that the draft bill he released on Thursday covers a topic that Foster is likely to pursue throughout the 120th Congress. He often asks the most questions about the use of AI in financial services at hearings and offers the most amendments related to the issue at markups.

Under the bill, model software would be developed for banking records and operations, regulatory reporting, stress testing, anti-money laundering and fraud screening, AI risk monitoring and other activities.

According to recent reports, the software must be open source, publicly available and tested for reliability and accuracy, according to the summary. It would be tested using synthetic or legally permitted historical data rather than actual customer accounts. Regulators would not take financial or supervisory actions during the study.

The software developed during the study would not have to be adopted; rather, it “should be viewed as a starting point for further modernization,” the summary indicates.

All software models would have to be published within one year of enactment of the bill and a final report assessing feasibility, costs and savings, competition and other criteria, would be due to Congress within two years.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Just like Wi-Fi-enabled lights and plugs and locks, smart thermostats give you the ability to automate an element of your home for increased convenience.
  • Using a companion app on your phone, you get intuitive and nuanced controls, including the ability to customize temperature schedules remotely.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Just like Wi-Fi-enabled lights and plugs and locks, smart thermostats give you the ability to automate an element of your home for increased convenience. In this case, it’s your temperature controls. These devices tend to be a bit pricier than conventional thermostats, but it’s an upgrade that can pay for itself over time thanks to increased energy efficiency.

Using a companion app on your phone, you get intuitive and nuanced controls, including the ability to customize temperature schedules remotely. That comes in handy when, let’s say, you want to warm up the house earlier than usual if you head home from work early. You’re also able to track your usage with monthly energy reports, which can help you bring down your bills.

According to recent reports, for the past few months, my colleagues and I have been steadily testing smart thermostats throughout in our homes, including models from Google Nest, ecobee, and Honeywell Home. These are the models we tried, plus a few more we recommend based on our research and reviews. We’ve also included some expert advice on what to consider before you buy.

The ecobee covers the standard lineup of smart thermostat features, with climate control and money-saving that are commonplace among any of the top options, but sets itself apart with a wider range of smart features.

According to recent reports, it doubles as a security base for your home security, serving as the arming and disarming mechanism. It also features a built-in air quality monitor that alerts you to poor air quality and sends reminders when you need to replace air filters in your furnace.

In a recent development, the ecobee comes with a separate smart sensor for precision control, allowing it to fine-tune the temperature in the rooms where you spend the most time. Though it comes with a single sensor, you can purchase more to add that precision throughout the house.

It also provides free Eco+ Software which works on your smartphone and generates energy reports that further maximize your energy savings.

It has been revealed that the smart thermostat also comes with a host of standard smart features. After connecting to a Google assistant or Alexa, the smart speaker built directly on the thermostat itself can take voice commands and even play music. It also comes with a three-year warranty from date of purchase.

Each purchase comes with a full converter kit as well, so if you aren’t at the moment in a home with a C-Wire, you can add one by following the kit instructions.

According to recent reports, for a smart thermostat that better fits a tight budget, Amazon has its own option that comes with many of the same energy-saving features at a lower overall price tag. Through the connected app, the thermostat tracks and reports your energy usage and peak time periods throughout the week and month.

Through Alexa, you can also set home, away, and sleep temperatures that you can schedule throughout the day and week in order to further maximize savings on your energy bill and optimize your air conditioning to your exact schedule. You can also set the temperature remotely from your phone through the Alexa app.

Beyond the controls, by using an Amazon product, the company will pass along potential rebate and saving opportunities that you could take advantage of by owning a smart thermostat.

As for upfront costs, the device is designed specifically for easy DIY installation so there is no need to hire an HVAC technician unless you want one.

The Honeywell T9 is a great choice if your primary concern is reducing energy use and lowering your bills. You need to pair it with one of Honeywell’s smart room sensors to take advantage of the thermostat’s full functionality, which is an extra hurdle, but the sensor only costs about $30, so it’s a short one.

One of the key ways the T9 saves money is through virtual fencing. Using your phone’s GPS, the thermostat automatically switches between home and away mode as you come and go. So, when you leave your house, energy usage is reduced across the board.

In a recent development, honeywell also provides monthly usage reports that point out areas where energy can be reduced for a lower upfront cost. Adding more room sensors can increase the accuracy of those reports, giving you more chances to optimize your heating and cooling system.

The Honeywell T9 doesn’t have the same wide spectrum of features as our other recommendations, but it’s core functionality is very solid.

Sources indicate that the newest generation of the Google Nest Thermostat has impressed our team as an easy-to-install, easy-to-use option that reduces energy use and is compatible with most HVAC systems. Like previous models, the smart thermostat builds a schedule, learns your temperature preferences, and reduces energy when it isn’t needed.

Sources indicate that reviews Editor Danny Perez installed the Nest in his own home and absolutely fell in the love with nearly every aspect of it. “To say I like this thermostat is an understatement: It lights up when I pass by to show me the interior temps, as well as local weather and humidity (it’s nice to know my presence is acknowledged, not gonna lie),” writes Perez.

Beyond the basic features, Perez also pointed out how much he likes the actual display and design of the thermostat. “Sure, other thermostats and window a/c units have similar smart features, but they don’t blend into my home the way the Google Nest thermostat does. I genuinely enjoy looking at it. I light up when I pass by it.”.

Read Full Nest Thermostat Review.

Sources indicate that with a large, responsive touch screen, this basic Honeywell thermostat is easy to see from across the room, thanks to a large, custom-color display. It’s a versatile option, compatible with multiple smart home assistants. Like other models, it’s Energy Star-certified, which means that using one can help you save even more money through local rebates.

Sources indicate that while the smart thermostat is great for easy scheduling and reading, it lacks the learning software of the Google Nest or the virtual fencing adjustments that many other smart thermostats have. That said, it’s also considerably cheaper.

According to recent reports, most smart thermostats aren’t compatible with baseboard heating and cooling systems. This Mysa unit is the rare exception, and designed specifically to work with electric baseboards. Combine that with compatibility across every major smart home system, and the Mysa becomes one of very few thermostats with such capabilities.

While the compatibility alone makes this a tempting choice, it also has many of the same high-end smart features as the competition. This includes virtual fencing, so when you head out for the day, the thermostat automatically reduces energy use.

According to recent reports, another key feature is its temperature monitor. Unlike many other devices, which only provide you with degrees, the Mysa smart thermostat also measures and reports humidity levels.

Traditional thermostats only require power through the four classic wires while smart thermostats typically require low- voltage power all day in order to run the display screen and some basic functions. This low-voltage power comes from an additional fifth wire called the “common” wire or C-Wire. The biggest potential concern you may have with installation is if your home lacks this wire.

It has been revealed that if this is the case, it’s probably time to step away from your weekend home project and call an HVAC technician. While installing a common wire isn’t an incredibly difficult undertaking if you’re somewhat handy, it’s one that likely requires the expertise of a trained professional.

Some smart thermostats include installation kits that provide equipment and step-by-step instructions for adding a C-Wire to your current wiring. This can be a helpful addition to the handier among us, and may circumvent the need for an HVAC technician entirely, though you may want to keep one waiting in the wings if anything goes wrong.

Once you've wired and installed your smart thermostat, you can connect it to other devices in your home via Wi-Fi or occasionally Z-Wave. Most units are compatible with many major smart home ecosystems. While they’re compatible with many systems, I would still take a moment to check and make sure that a thermostat works specifically with the smart home setup you use at home.

Industry observers note that along with scheduling heating or cooling programs from the convenience of your phone, there are a handful of features that set smart thermostats apart from their traditional counterparts. Most smart models automatically adjust the temperature based on peak usage and some automatically respond to outdoor temperatures and set ideal temperatures indoors.

Sources indicate that other models use geofencing, or virtual fencing technology. This creates a radius around your home and detects how close or far away your smartphone is from it. With this, the smart thermostat eases energy use when you aren’t home, and ramps back up as you reenter the virtual boundary.

Several smart thermostats we cover use external sensors to expand the reach of temperature readings. Setup is typically no more complicated than placing the sensors around the house and syncing them up with the rest of the system.

Recent findings suggest that they’re great for maintaining different temperatures in rooms, like keeping bedrooms and bathrooms warm and offices and laundry rooms cool. More precise temperature control also increases the potential for saving energy. Smart thermostats that include sensors as part of their systems often come with one, though some models require purchasing sensors separately.

The Popular Mechanics Gear Team has tested several of these recommendations over the course of several months, including the ecobee Smart Thermostat Premium and the Google Nest Learning Thermostat. We installed these smart thermostats in our homes, set them up, and used them to keep ourselves warm and cool, as the seasons demanded. We gave them our seal of approval based on ease-of-use, installation process, programmable features, and how well the devices integrated with our smart home assistants, mobile devices, and tablets.

A few thermostats, such as the Honeywell Home Smart Color Thermostat, made the list despite the fact that we haven’t tested them yet. In those cases, we picked options from established brands with the specs and features that are comparable to our tested recommendations, and have received strong reviews from customers at online retailers.

We also prioritized options that were highly compatible with other smart devices and offered convenient features for everyday use. Price rice was a major consideration, as well: We chose models ranging from roughly $160 to $250, ensuring that we recommend a range of options that fit every need and budget.

It has been revealed that tom Price is a reviews editor for Popular Mechanics while also contributing to Runner's World, Best Products, and Bicycling.
