Longtime West Virginia Sen. Rockefeller dies

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1835 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rockefeller IV, D-W.Va., questions witnesses during a Senate Finance hearing on health care on June 23, 2011.
  • Jay Rockefeller, a five-term West Virginia Democrat and champion for the rural poor, has died at the age of 89.
  • Rockefeller, who retired after the 2014 elections, played key roles on the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee, where he helped write landmark children’s health insurance legislation, as well as the Commerce, Science and Transportation and Intelligence panels which he chaired.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sen. John D. Rockefeller IV, D-W.Va., questions witnesses during a Senate Finance hearing on health care on June 23, 2011. (Scott J. Ferrell/CQ Roll Call).

Former Sen. Jay Rockefeller, a five-term West Virginia Democrat and champion for the rural poor, has died at the age of 89.

Rockefeller, who retired after the 2014 elections, played key roles on the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee, where he helped write landmark children’s health insurance legislation, as well as the Commerce, Science and Transportation and Intelligence panels which he chaired.

Sources indicate that A staunchly progressive lawmaker, he represented a deeply conservative state that turned further to the right in his later years. Rockefeller, scion of a famous Latest York family renowned for its wealth, never wavered in his convictions and retired rather than face a potential backlash from voters upset by the then-Obama administration’s attempts to rein in the coal industry.

Sources indicate that sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who challenged Rockefeller for his seat before he decided not to seek reelection, released a statement Friday praising her predecessor’s legacy.

Sources indicate that “Jay dedicated his life to serving West Virginia and our nation, leaving a lasting legacy. He was always a true gentleman who treated me with respect, kindness, and encouragement,” Capito said. “Over the years, we developed a wonderful friendship that transcended politics, and I will always be grateful for that.”.

West Virginia’s Republican Gov. Patrick Morrisey — himself a transplanted Northerner, with roots in Brooklyn and Latest Jersey — lauded Rockefeller’s record on health care and aid for coal miners and veterans in their adopted state.

“His work helped shape our state and left a lasting mark on the lives of generations of West Virginians,” Morrisey said.

According to recent reports, rockefeller was born in Fresh York City on June 18, 1937, the great-grandson of Standard Oil Co. founder John D. Rockefeller, who was once considered the world’s richest man. Rockefeller attended Harvard University, graduating with an A.B. in 1961. His passion was for the Far East and he spent three years studying at the International Christian University in Tokyo.

Sources indicate that he returned to the states and was appointed by President John F. Kennedy to the National Advisory Council of the Peace Corps in 1961, spearheaded the Peace Corps initial program in the Philippines. He worked for a brief time in what was then known as U.S. Department of Far Eastern Affairs before deciding to embark on a public service role of a more personal nature. He enrolling as a VISTA volunteer, in the program which would later be known as AmeriCorps, and moved to the small mining community of Emmons, W.Va., in 1964 at age 27.

It has been revealed that in West Virginia, Rockefeller found his life’s work. He described the experience as being “reborn,” and spoke often the poverty and hardship he encountered living in the small town. “I could not leave,” he said of West Virginia. “I [had] become so devoted to those people and the unfairness.".

He had planned to remain only one year, but decided to stay and became active in local politics. He broke from his family's long tradition of Republican loyalty and ran successfully for the House of Delegates as a Democrat in 1966. Two years later, he was elected secretary of state.

Industry observers note that rockefeller lost a bid for governor in 1972, but he became the president of West Virginia Wesleyan College and continued to place roots in the state. He married Sharon Percy Rockefeller in 1967 and they started their family. When he ran for governor again in 1976, he won, and served two terms before winning election to the U.S. Senate in 1984, ultimately serving five terms before retiring in 2014.

Rockefeller was determined to increase economic opportunities for West Virginia, for whom he felt was forgotten and abandoned by the rest of the country. He called the people of his state “the hardest-working people I know,” and believed that bringing more business opportunities would help lift the state out of severe rural poverty and the dependence on the coal industry.

Rockefeller traveled to Japan and worked tirelessly to bring a Toyota manufacturing plant to Buffalo, W.Va, one of over twenty Japanese companies he’d brought to West Virginia. He fought for fair trade policies and targeted tax relief to protect West Virginia industries such as steel and chemicals.

Coal mining had long been the economic backbone of West Virginia, but Rockefeller felt more must be done to protect miners, many of whom worked in unsafe conditions or fell ill with pneumoconiosis, or black lung disease, after years of inhaling coal dust.

It has been revealed that but defying the coal industry came with a political cost. When Rockefeller originally ran for governor in 1972, he had opposed mountaintop mining, also called strip mining, or the practice of removing large amounts of earth and rock in order to access underground seams of coal. When he ran again in 1976, he reversed his position and won.

But even as he ascended to the Senate, Rockefeller remained both friend and foe to the coal industry.

Despite growing up on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, figuratively and literally hundreds of miles away from coal mines, Rockefeller understood its deep roots in West Virginia’s economy and culture. He believed it was the miners — rather than industry — for whom he was defending.

He hung a century-old photo of a coal miner in his Senate office in the Hart building, and would point to the photo and remark to visitors that “this is why I’m here and who I work for.”.

Rockefeller fought to secure pensions for miners, especially as coal companies would file for bankruptcy and immediately restructure to do away with pension prepares.

Industry observers note that in 1990, Rockefeller was one of only 11 senators to vote against the bipartisan Clean Air Act, which he felt disadvantaged workers in West Virginia. But those close to him said the decision weighed heavily on him, and Rockefeller privately worried that the lack of such regulations would pollute the air and destroy waterways, the brunt of which would be born by the same disadvantaged people whom he vowed to protect.

It has been revealed that he believed strongly in the deliberative aspects of the legislative process, consuming great amounts of reading material to familiarize himself with the problems. During a time of increasing partisan rancor, Rockefeller still reached across the aisle to find a willing partner, even when there was not one to be found.

In 2010, as the Environmental Protection Agency’s greenhouse gas regulations were coming to fruition, Rockefeller came up with a compromise to delay implementation for two years.

It has been revealed that he viewed himself as a broker between industry interests and the hard working people from coal-states like West Virginia. He had hoped that his years of standing up for coal miners and West Virginia interests would foster enough goodwill among industries primed to oppose any compromise that was less than an all-out rejection of the existing EPA statutes.

But industry walked away from Rockefeller, preferring a hard-line opposition to EPA regulations, and lobbied other senators to vote against Rockefeller’s measure. Furious, Rockefeller took to the floor of the Senate to denounce the coal industry and its leaders, an unprecedented action for a popular coal-state senator.

In a recent development, “The reality is that many who run the coal industry today would rather attack false enemies and deny real problems then find solutions,” he said on the Senate floor in June 2012. “Scare tactics are a cynical waste of time, money and, worst of all, coal miners’ hopes. But sadly, these coal operators have closed themselves off from any other opposing voices and few dared to speak out for change — even though it’s been staring them in the face for years.”.

His fury against the coal industry was heard loudly, many speculating that he would retire rather than face reelection.

Industry observers note that he had won reelection to the Senate handily during his five campaigns. In 2008, his final election, he was reelected with nearly 64 percent of the vote. But six months following his fated coal speech, in January 2013, Rockefeller declared he would retire at the end of his fifth term.

Sources indicate that rockefeller’s legacy may best be known for his fight to expand health care for vulnerable populations, including children, the economically disadvantaged and the elderly. Rockefeller served as one of the chief congressional champions for President Bill Clinton’s proposed health care overhaul, and later he played a critical role and was a loud progressive voice in writing and passing the Affordable Care Act in the Senate.

Rockefeller believed strongly in a public health insurance option, offering it as an amendment in the Senate Finance Committee during the ACA markup. A public-run insurance plan, he said, would put patients before profits, and help those people, especially West Virginians, with high health care costs and poor coverage who were left “out in the cold.”.

Recent findings suggest that "These are people," Rockefeller noted, visibly emotional during his closing arguments to the Senate Finance Committee. "Eleven-year-old kids. These are families, and we have to respect them. And you respect them by giving them a choice.".

Recent findings suggest that the amendment was rejected. Rockefeller pivoted to strengthening Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program provisions, believing that poor and disadvantaged families could seek refuge within those programs. CHIP had been one of Rockefeller’s signature legislative victories, helping to write that program initially in 1997 and later working on a major expansion that became law in 2009.

Despite his initial concerns and later disappointments — at one time saying publicly he could not support the measure as it stood — he later added his support to the ACA, citing it as a win for all Americans and actively lobbied his colleagues to support it.

Rockefeller was also known for his role on the Senate Intelligence Committee. A former chairman, he was critical of the nation's mismanagement of the Iraq war and clashed frequently with Republicans over the treatment of detainees. After he retired from Congress, Rockefeller served as a distinguished fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.

Recent findings suggest that respect for Rockefeller ran deep on Capitol Hill. He was beloved by staff and known as a thoughtful, deliberative lawmaker. He had a fondness for classical music and served as a board member of the Bach Consort, an organization in Washington devoted to the study and performance of the music of Bach and his contemporaries. He admired art and Asian culture, and served as a board member of the Asia Society.

Rockefeller is survived by his wife, Sharon Percy Rockefeller; four children: John D. Rockefeller V, Valerie Rockefeller, Charles Rockefeller and Justin Rockefeller; and nine grandchildren.

Disclosure: the author served as a staffer in Rockefeller’s Senate office from 2009-11.

The Secret Reason Why Ancient Roman Concrete Is So Remarkably Strong—And How One Engineer Has Recreated It

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1030 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • The Pantheon, Rome’s unreinforced concrete dome, constructed around 118 to 125 C.E., still stands intact to this day.
  • Sources indicate that for decades, researchers credited the inclusion of volcanic ash from Pozzuoli, a city in Naples, Italy, for the unique strength in the mix; others claimed that lime, a calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide binder created from heating limestone, was the key ingredient.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

The Pantheon, Rome’s unreinforced concrete dome, constructed around 118 to 125 C.E., still stands intact to this day. The Aqua Virgo, part of the ancient Roman system of aqueducts, was built in 19 B.C.E., yet still supplies Roman fountains, including Trevi, today. Is it any wonder that ancient Rome still draws our global admiration?

Sources indicate that for decades, researchers credited the inclusion of volcanic ash from Pozzuoli, a city in Naples, Italy, for the unique strength in the mix; others claimed that lime, a calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide binder created from heating limestone, was the key ingredient. Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Admir Masic, a civil and environmental engineering professor, thought there must be more to the story.

Industry observers note that masic established a lab at MIT with the specific goal of researching ancient Roman concrete. First and foremost a chemist, he indicates he knew there was something beneath the surface of Roman concrete potentially lending it strength. His team of researchers, from MIT, Harvard, Italy, and Switzerland, discovered that ancient Roman concrete gets its strength—and therefore its incredible longevity—from its inherent self-healing properties. As cracks form, the surrounding material somehow fills them back in, over and over.

According to recent reports, scientists commonly suspected that ash, and not lime, was the hero of the Roman concrete-making process, because the Romans were the first to add volcanic ash to the mixture. This hydration-based method gives the mixture additional strength and makes it possible to build in all seasons.

But it didn’t explain the self-healing quality. Another mystery was in the concrete’s apparent crystalline phases, known to take shape only at high temperatures—at least 80 degrees Celsius (or about 176 degrees Fahrenheit). Yet, the Romans wouldn’t have exposed their concrete mixture to those sorts of temperatures.

Then, researchers discovered calcium aluminate hydrate being used as a binding agent in ancient Roman concrete, which only created further intrigue. This is where the mystery of self-healing gained its first big clue—trying to learn where the calcium came from, Masic states. So his team’s focus shifted to the overlooked role of lime, which is primarily composed of calcium compounds.

In a recent development, masic notes that modern concrete, when mixed with lime, volcanic components, and water, creates a homogeneous mixture—quite unlike ancient Roman concrete, which is studded with tiny, distinct white particles. “How is it possible that every construction site would make this heterogeneous material even though they put so much effort [into] making it very standard in terms of ingredients [and] how to mix it?” Masic wondered.

It has been revealed that the research team decided to investigate the mechanical, structural, and chemical properties of these particles, dubbed “lime clasts,” which were present in every sample they analyzed, Masic states. It led the team to realize “that lime clasts are not an error in mixing, or sloppy mixing, but they are the root of a very specific way of mixing mortars.” Not present in modern concrete, but ubiquitous in the ancient Roman version.

Originally, researchers believed that the Romans added water to the lime mixture to make a slurry. This “slaking” creates a homogeneously structured mixture. However, the presence of the lime clasts didn’t fit into this model.

In a recent development, what the Romans actually did was “hot mixing,” which introduces a novel series of chemical reactions. They ground the stone into tiny pieces of calcium oxide and mixed them with volcanic ash and a dry aggregate. Finally, they added water. “This is where the reaction of calcium oxide with water happens, and the entire mix gets hot, [which] releases energy, and creates hot spots up to 200 to 250 degrees Celsius,” Masic explains.

While lime and the ash formed the basis of the mixture, the constellation of millimeter-scale, mineral particles embedded throughout the mortar turned out to be the secret outcome of the hot mixing process. The key to hot mixing is that it doesn’t dissolve all of the lime clasts. Instead, they get systematically embedded into the concrete mix, creating a reservoir of calcium. When the concrete is exposed to water, the calcium spontaneously expands, creating a protective layer of nanoparticles that fill in the cracks before they can spread. Voila, self-healing concrete. Masic’s team published their findings in the journal Science Advances.

It has been revealed that the team’s own recreation of Roman concrete healed a crack within two weeks. A modern concrete mixture didn’t heal at all, allowing water to flow through the crack. Eventually, water seepage like this destroys the integrity of modern concrete structures.

It has been revealed that roman self-healing concrete allows the mixture to last longer and requires less maintenance and less latest material for construction—which also reduces emissions during concrete production. Standard cement production, the solid binder in concrete, accounts for about 8 percent of global CO2 emissions today.

Industry observers note that our world actually has various forms of self-healing concrete, such as bioconcrete, in which bacterial spores activate and produce calcium carbonate to fill in cracks. However, the high costs of modern methods keep the industry from using them widely, indicates Masic. Meanwhile the ancient Roman method offers “self-healing at an extremely competitive price,” he says.

Now that we know the secret, should we return to making concrete this way?

In a recent development, in fact, Masic co-founded a company in 2021, that uses lessons he has learned from studying ancient Roman concrete. Today, DMAT is creating a concrete additive “that increases the lifespan of concrete structures by 50 percent and reduces CO2 emissions to 40% of traditional concrete,” according to MIT’s Climate Portal. As of August 2026, their material is part of underground water tanks, road barriers, and pavement in Italy and Switzerland. DMAT also aims to expand to U.S. infrastructure projects.

Manasee Wagh contributed to this story.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stephen Miller, White House deputy chief of staff, talks with reporters at the White House on April 28. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

President Donald Trump on Friday confirmed that Stephen Miller, the architect of the hard-line immigration and deportation program voters rejected this week, will become White House chief of staff.

Susie Wiles will depart that post and move to the Trump political organization, which appears to be in full operation, even after the president's last midterm election. Miller has been deputy chief of staff, overseeing the Trump administration's domestic policy.

Miller’s first day will be Monday, Trump noted in a social media post.

Trump dubbed Miller “one of my most trusted advisors” and noted Wiles, who also oversaw his 2024 presidential campaign, “has done an outstanding job.”.

Wiles, who Trump recently declared had won a battle with breast cancer, remarked in a X post that “serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime,” adding she was “proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.”.

The chief-of-staff change came three days after Republicans were demolished in Trump’s final midterm election, with House Democrats on pace for the largest majority in over a decade and at least a 54-seat Senate majority come January.

Trump addressed the personnel move as he departed the White House Friday for an event and weekend in Florida — though he ignored a question about his recent declaration that Wiles would be sticking around.

Industry observers note that “I wanted to make a change,” he mentioned in a roughly three-minute exchange with reporters before he walked to Marine One. “Sometimes in life, you have to make moves.”.

Recent findings suggest that trump in recent days had become open to working with Democrats after the new Congress is seated on Jan. 3, even after railing against what he called the party’s “bad” policy during an October-long campaign rally blitz.

“Look, I mean, I'll get along, probably, with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive,” Trump told reporters Wednesday. “But I have the power of the veto. So if we don't like what they're doing… They've already called and they want to talk about things. And that's fine.”.

Trump summoned Thursday's press pool into the Oval Office for an executive order signing. On his desk was a red baseball cap with "VETO" across the front in large white lettering.

According to recent reports, miller has worked on Capitol Hill as an aide to several GOP lawmakers, including former Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., who became attorney general in Trump's first administration.

But making the hard-line Miller his White House chief of staff even before congressional Democrats get organized likely will draw the ire of the incoming majority.

Recent findings suggest that virginia Rep. Donald S. Beyer Jr. was among the first Democratic lawmakers to slam Trump’s decision.

“Trump’s elevation of Stephen Miller doubles down on the politics of hatred, lawlessness, and failure that the American people soundly rejected three days ago,” Beyer said in a statement. "Miller embodies the worst elements of the Trump presidency. His promotion shows that Trump has learned nothing from his electoral debacle and has no intention of even trying to work constructively with the next Congress.”.

Many congressional Democrats — leaders, returning incumbents and members-elect — want to investigate Trump, his inner circle and family members while also pursuing a legislative agenda aimed at paring the cost of living.

In a recent development, to that end, as chief of staff, Democrat-run committees calling Miller to testify is highly unlikely since he could continue to claim executive privilege. That allows senior White House aides to withhold many internal West Wing communications, documents, and presidential-related conversations and actions, from lawmakers.

In public comments and television interviews, Miller has accused Democrats of being aligned with figures and candidates who “hate” Americans, and once stated the party is “unworthy of power.”.

Sources indicate that “So the Democrats have become a party of freaks, weirdos, losers and crazies,” Miller mentioned during a July appearance on Fox News. “But you can’t laugh it off because it’s deadly serious. When you give these people power, everything you know and love in this world falls apart. You have chaos, corruption, decay, violence, poverty.”.

The only thing worse than discovering your car has a dead battery is having it happen when it’s raining. I also appreciate that it includes spark-proof and reverse-polarity protection, an output port for charging portable electronics, and a six-mode flashlight.

Recent findings suggest that that mentioned, the GB40 isn’t perfect. While I found that it punched above its weight in jump-starting power and its battery life is adequate, it isn’t the most powerful portable jump starter among those I’ve recently tested, and its 2,150 milliampere-hour (mAh) capacity is definitely on the lower side. It also doesn’t have an LED screen but rather uses lights as indicators of its status and operation. Even more crucially, it uses a manual override function to boost severely depleted batteries instead of a dedicated boost button.

It has been revealed that I tested the Noco Boost Plus GB40 over several months in Oregon spanning the wet and dry seasons. When testing a portable jump starter, I evaluate how quickly it starts a vehicle, how many jump-starts it provides before needing to be recharged, how easy it is to use, its features, and the number and effectiveness of its auxiliary power ports to charge portable devices such as a smartphone.

It has been revealed that the Noco GB40 easily fits in the palm of my hand, and the rubberized case and ribs built into each side make it easy to grip, which is notable when working around an engine with moving parts. Its small size also means it’s easier to store in a vehicle’s glove box than a larger device like the Gooloo GT6000, which I recommend as the best portable jump starter for most people.

According to recent reports, the Noco GB40 doesn’t have an LED screen like many of the portable jump starters from Gooloo, its main competitor. But the touch-based control panel on one side makes it relatively simple to operate. This consists of a large power button with a white on/off LED next to it, a four-segment multicolor battery-level indicator that reveals the state of charge in 25 percent increments, an error indicator, a boost LED, a manual override button, and a button for the flashlight.

Industry observers note that with a peak output of only 1,000 amps, the Noco Boost Plus GB40 is the least powerful portable jump starter among those I’ve tested. Its 2,150 mAh rating also makes it the lowest in reserve-power capacity. That stated, it had no challenges jump-starting my Honda Element when I left the lights on and drained the battery. It even cranked the 6.8-liter V10 in my RV when I came back to it after months in storage and found the battery depleted.

Sources indicate that I also intentionally left it powered on (since it doesn’t have an automatic shutoff like the Astro AI S8, which I recommend for its value) and it lasted about 24 hours before shutting down. Via a 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-C input, it charges about as fast as other portable jump starters with the same specs, and it took just under four hours to charge from 0 to 100 percent using the supplied USB-C cable.

According to recent reports, among features, the flashlight on the GB40 is the most compelling. It has six modes, including an SOS and strobe, which puts it well ahead of the competition. It also has two lenses, one on each side of the output ports, whereas most portable jump starters use a single flashlight lens. While the flashlight isn’t as bright as some others at 100 lumens (for comparison, the $70 Gooloo GP2000, has a 400-lumen flashlight), I found the Noco GB40 more than adequate for use at night.

Industry observers note that the Noco GB40’s USB-C charging input doesn’t double as an output port to charge portable devices, which puts it at a disadvantage. It has just one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A output port for charging portable electronics (the Gooloo GP2000 has two) and charged my iPhone 16 from 0 percent to 80 percent in about two hours.

Instead of a boost button that supplies a bit more amperage to jump-start a very dead battery, the GB40 has a manual override button that, when pushed and held for three seconds, detects a severely depleted battery (below three volts).

It’s a far less user-friendly feature, plus it disables the Noco’s automatic spark-proof and reverse-polarity protection. As such, people need to be extra careful not to allow the cable clamps to touch, which can cause dangerous sparking. To complicate things further, the GB40 has an LED labeled “boost” that’s simply an indicator light to let you know the device is properly connected to the battery.

According to recent reports, there are certainly much more powerful portable jump starters than the Noco Boost Plus GB40 and much of the competition offers features that are far more convenient (albeit for a higher price point), perhaps most significantly, a boost button. Above all, the GB40’s waterproof rating is the best reason to buy it, plus its compact size, six-mode flashlight, and emergency charging for small devices make it an appealing choice. It also provides ample and reliable power to give a dead battery in most vehicles a boost and start the engine.

Shop Noco Boost Plus GB40 Portable Jump Starter.

Other Portable Jump Starters We Recommend.

The Gooloo GT6000 packs 27,000 mAh of reserve power capacity and 6,000-amp peak current. This allows it to jump-start vehicles ranging from a small motorcycle to a heavy-duty truck with a 12.0-liter diesel engine. The GT6000 offers a standby time of two years, and it’s ready to jump-start a vehicle after just seven minutes of recharging. It’s got a heap of charging ports, including a 100-watt USB-C in/out that can top off the internal battery from empty to full in 1.4 hours. The device’s 3.2-inch screen makes checking battery level, charging output, and more easy and foolproof.

Industry observers note that with 4,000 amps of peak current and 24,000 mAh of capacity, the Wolfbox can jump-start up to 10.0-liter gas or 6.0-liter diesel engines. It holds a charge for more than a year. The 1.5-cubic-foot-per-minute air pump takes one minute to inflate a 17-inch tire from 30 to 36 psi. It also has a 65-watt USB-C in/out port to rapidly recharge the internal battery, two USB-A ports to charge other devices, and a 400-lumen, three-mode LED flashlight.

It has been revealed that the Noco AX65 combines a portable jump starter and a portable air compressor into a single device. The jump starter has an impressive 16,000 mAh capacity and delivers 2,000 amps of peak power. The tire inflator pumps out 2.3 cubic feet per minute of airflow. The jump starter cranks gas engines up to 8.0 liters and diesel engines up to 6.0 liters. The tire inflator has a digital display, auto shutoff, and memory settings like other air compressors I’ve tested but also pauses and then resumes inflation when a set pressure is reached to ensure proper inflation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that it feels like yesterday we were busy powerwashing the patio, mulching, and prepping the grill for the first cookout of the summer. But lo and behold, winter is coming. And as someone who absolutely hates the cold, this isn’t necessarily a welcoming experience. But as I’ve gotten older, I’ve embraced layering. This is especially important for the more physical parts of my day-to-day, where I need to add and subtract as I go.

I used to be a two-jacket kind of guy—something for fall/spring and a big, bulky winter parka for winter. Now that I test workwear and outerwear, my entire concept of staying warm has changed. I’ve moved on to waxed canvas, corduroy, and merino wool. I still wear down from time to time, but I do it strategically.

With the cold weather upon us, I went through some of the best ways to gear up for the winter without going full George Costanza GORE-TEX. These options are sleek, lightweight, and can be worn over additional layers as you see fit. Let’s get into it.

Flint and Tinder’s waxed trucker is my go-to, but there are some slightly warmer options that add a little extra bulk without going too overboard. The Flannel-Lined Quilted Waxed Rancher Jacket fits the bill perfectly. It’s designed with a slightly heavier 10-ounce Martexin sailcloth, waxed on both sides for warmth, and a cozy flannel lining stuffed with 4 ounces of insulation for “chillier” conditions.

Carhartt is a workwear icon and a staple among our editors. Some of its vintage jackets fetch a surprising price on the secondary market, so they're always a worthwhile investment. If you’re looking for something winter-ready, the Washed Duc Active Jac should be your go-to. It features 80g Thinsulate for warmth without too much bulk, and Cordura-reinforced sleeve hems add durability for that classic Carhartt workwear touch.

Barbour’s iconic Bedale Waxed Jacket will cost a little more, but it’s worth every penny. It offers exceptional weather resistance and insulation, keeping you warmer than its weight suggests. The Raglan sleeves give you a little more range of motion and make it ideal for layering. It also features both zip and stud closures for increased protection and insulation from the elements. It might also be the best-looking jacket on this list—especially if you prefer the old-school waxed look.

Levi’s is about as classic as it gets, and its Depot Jacket is essentially iconic. It’s one of the warmer workwear-forward jackets on this list, without the bulk. The quilted, lined interior provides much-needed insulation, and the cotton canvas shell is durable and hard-wearing. The corduroy collar gives it bonus points for style (not to mention a real throwback look). You can never go wrong with Levi’s.

Recent findings suggest that yeti isn’t the name most closely associated with outerwear, but the brand has been expanding. First, with its newly introduced line of iPhone cases, and lo and behold, Yeti jackets are now a thing. This down jacket is surprisingly light, and like most of its coolers, tumblers, and ramblers, is supremely insulated. $400 is a little pricey for a down jacket, but in typical Yeti fashion, well worth the extra dough.

In a recent development, corduroy is more of a fall staple, but it still works well as a layering option into early winter. The Piston Trucker Jacket from Reigning Champ features a stylish waist cut, a plush, textured feel, and an adjustable bottom-tab hem for a more customized fit. Layer a simple flannel underneath or add a hoodie for extra warmth. If you choose the latter, though, you may want to size up. And like most, if not all, of the outerwear on this list, this one only gets better the more you wear it.

It has been revealed that patagonia has winter wear down pat, and if you’re looking for something in the fleece department, its latest Retro-X Fleece Jacket is calling your name. It gives off an old-school fleece vibe, but it feels even warmer than it looks, thanks to its NetPlus 100% postconsumer recycled nylon made from old fishing nets. It also features zip-up hand-warmer side pockets, mobile Y-Joint sleeves, and an internal wind flap to keep you protected from the elements.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re really looking to go fancy (and warm), Overland’s array of sheepskin jackets will have you looking and feeling like Rocky training in Siberia, or at least its vintage-inspired sheepskin bomber jacket will. It boasts a convertible notch-to-stand-up collar with two buckle straps, adjustable waist straps for a more form-fitting fit, and four total pockets with plenty of storage. You won’t have to layer up with this one—and like most of our favorite outerwear, it only gets better with age.

This week: Lame duck kicks off with Hegseth impeachment effort

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thomas Massie of Kentucky told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session.
  • The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.
  • Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the newly introduced Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Departing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.

Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the newly introduced Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the expected next speaker of the House, said Sunday that he would support the Hegseth impeachment.

“I'm a hard 'yes' on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries stated on ABC’s “This Week.” “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe. Pete Hegseth has got to go.”.

Industry observers note that departing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session.

In a recent development, it’s also orientation week on Capitol Hill for new members of Congress. House orientation got underway Sunday.

The Senate, meanwhile, looks to take up a bipartisan permitting bill that has the backing of President Donald Trump.

“This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

Senate negotiators over the weekend released text of an amendment seeking to address remaining concerns.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m grateful for the input throughout this process from Senate and House colleagues, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders. Our manager’s amendment improves [the bill] and addresses the thoughtful feedback we have received,” Senate Environment and Public Works ranking Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island said in a statement. “Now it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build massive things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs.”.

Beyond the permitting bill, the Senate Republican majority may seek to use its remaining time trying to confirm more of Trump’s nominations before the control of the floor agenda passes to the Democrats.

"We've got the farm bill, the NDAA, and we have that third reconciliation bill that we need to get across the finish line, and there are so many things that we need to get done and buttoned up," including nominations, departing Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., said in a weekend Fox News interview. Blackburn, one of the Republicans who had success at the ballot box, is now governor-elect of Tennessee. But it's an open question how long lawmakers will want to stick around.

Recent findings suggest that there’s also the matter of an imminent fight over funding the government and laying the groundwork for the fresh Congress. Republican leadership elections are scheduled for Tuesday, while Democratic leadership elections are expected in December. Democratic senators-elect are due on Capitol Hill Monday and Tuesday, according to the office of Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. Schumer is widely expected to be the majority leader in 2027.

There have been some calls for Senate Republicans to delay their elections, though current Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota has been widely expected to remain as the Republican leader.

It has been revealed that “One of the things I learned in business and the Army is that after a failure, you have to start with honesty, transparency, and accountability,” Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., remarked in a Sunday night statement. “As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward.”.

In a recent development, sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., has also been circulating a letter calling for a delay, and he has argued the election should not be held, in part, because the makeup of the Senate Republican Conference is not yet final. Senate races are still not called in Alaska and Mississippi.

Sources indicate that absent this week will be Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who recently had a stroke.

In a recent development, “The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far. In order to take my recovery seriously and get back to work on the quickest timeline possible, I will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital today,” Murphy said in a Friday statement.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • As the weather gets cold, you don’t have to pay an arm and a leg just to keep your limbs from freezing off.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

As the weather gets cold, you don’t have to pay an arm and a leg just to keep your limbs from freezing off. Instead of heating your entire home, simply plug in a space heater and get direct warmth from a nearby source. If you want a compact yet powerful option, the Lasko Whirlwind Heat Oscillating Space Heater is an ideal choice.

What I like so much about this Lasko is its combination of size, power, and oscillation. It is small enough to sit comfortably on my desk or nightstand without taking up too much space, yet in combination with the dual-axis oscillation and powerful heating, it can warm up an entire room.

Much like the Dreo Whole Room Heater, the Lasko is designed with dual-axis oscillation, meaning it oscillates both vertically and horizontally. It can also oscillate in both directions simultaneously for greater coverage of an entire space. As a result, the heater boasts a total coverage of up to 300 square feet, which should be more than enough for most bedrooms, offices, and even many living rooms.

Recent findings suggest that that design is backed by 1,500 watts of heating power. The heat comes at three different heating levels that adjust the fan power. On its highest level, the heating is almost abrasive up close. In a small room at our office, I felt a tangible difference in temperature around the entire room within minutes, and just as importantly, near-instant hot air from the second I turned it on.

My one complaint is that there isn’t a separate control for both heat levels and fan power, which could lead to a slightly more nuanced level of control. That remarked, the auto-eco mode allows you to set a specific temperature, which the space heater will reach, go on low heat mode until it is two degrees above the set temperature, and then shut off automatically.

Sources indicate that this makes it a lot easier to run without direct supervision or accidentally running it for hours on end. Similarly, there is a sleep mode as well where you can set a timer up to 12 hours so it will shut off after a set amount of time, making it great to use once you get in bed.

In a recent development, the Lasko packs all that power in a relatively compact body. In cases of cold streaks in my drafty office building, I can set it up to run on my desk without feeling like I’ve sacrificed all my working space just to stay warm. In fact, I can still have my laptop, books, and assorted gear strewn about.

According to recent reports, placed on the nightstand or on top of a dresser, it works perfectly to warm you up from bed as well. One of the small but notable features is the remote control. While not uncommon, I also love the remote control. I can place it on a stand or even in the corner of a room when I don’t want direct heat and still control the heat level, temperature setting, oscillation, sleep timer, and screen light.

The Lasko Whirlwind doesn’t have any specifically unique safety features, but it has everything you might need for peace of mind. The ceramic safety plug can handle high levels of wattage without overheating to prevent electrical fires, and the space heater will automatically shut off if the motor overheats or the body tips over. The overall housing surrounding the heater stays cool, so you won’t burn your hands if you need to touch it.

The Lasko Whirlwind does exactly what I want it to. I want powerful heat, customizable temperature settings, and quality safety features, and the Lasko provides that. The small size takes that powerful heat and puts it in a container that is compact enough to fit on desks, nightstands, or in the corner of your room.

It has been revealed that if you want a device powerful enough to heat up a full room but small enough to fit anywhere, the Lasko Whirlwind is an excellent choice. If you want to heat up large spaces, you might need something a bit larger, but very few space heaters have pound for pound as much power as this one.

#31189. The 6 Best Mini-LED TVs Deliver a Bright Screen and Great Value

The 6 Best Mini-LED TVs Deliver a Bright Screen and Great Value

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Mini-LED is among the most versatile display technologies ever created.
  • The best mini-LED TVs right now provide a brighter and more impactful picture than ever, especially since many of them get a performance boost from other display tech like quantum dots and the hot upcoming multicolored backlight configuration, RGB LED.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Mini-LED is among the most versatile display technologies ever created. By shrinking down the LED backlighting that powered older TVs since flat screens first gained traction in the late 2000s, TV makers have found a way to deliver brighter TVs with richer, more accurate colors without relying on expensive newly introduced display technologies.

The best mini-LED TVs right now provide a brighter and more impactful picture than ever, especially since many of them get a performance boost from other display tech like quantum dots and the hot upcoming multicolored backlight configuration, RGB LED.

In a recent development, just as importantly, they often offer great bang for the buck, especially when you're looking for a larger screen size—let’s say 75 inches or higher. As malleable as they are cost-effective, mini-LED is the secret sauce behind some of the best TVs on the market, even outdoing premium OLED screens in metrics like brightness and color expansion.

We’ve tested the top mini-LED TVs around, from entry-level options to groundbreaking flagships, to help you find the best options for your money.

In a recent development, I picked the top mini-LED TVs after sampling the best the market has to offer from brands like LG, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Hisense. I tested four of the TVs directly, while two of them were tested by Popular Mechanics staff and recommended based on that testing.

Industry observers note that my evaluation was based on performance traits like brightness, color vibrancy and accuracy, image processing and upscaling, black levels, and overall contrast. For my testing process, I used objective measurements like brightness and color accuracy with a Portrait Displays C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, a G1 pattern generator, and Calman software, as well as subjective testing using a wide library of familiar content, from test demos to films and TV shows via 4K HDR Blu-rays and streaming. I also weighed usability features like smarts and gaming options, overall design, and size options for those interested in the ever-expanding big-screen TV market.

Industry observers note that I’ve been reviewing TVs and audio technology for well over a decade at publications like Wired, Business Insider, Digital Trends, and others. I’ve reviewed virtually every kind of TV and display technology available, from budget screens to premium RGB LEDs. I’ve gone hands-on with the best new mini-LED TVs from brands like Samsung, LG, Sony, TCL, Hisense, Roku, and others, along with competing tech like OLED and QD-OLED, each of which has its advantages. Few things give me more pleasure than finding people the best tech for their money at every performance level and budget.

According to recent reports, RGB LED, which uses tri-colored red, green, and blue light clusters for enhanced color expression, was the hot latest display tech at the start of 2026. Virtually every major brand debuted some form of RGB Mini-LED, kick-starting a premium Mini-LED alternative to OLED.

Industry observers note that when TCL introduced its own RGB TV for 2026, the RM9L, it seemed less excited about the RGB factor, and more interested in hyping up its exclusive new mini-LED tech, Super Quantum Dots (SQD). The QM8L makes it easy to see why.

In a recent development, SQD is an advanced version of regular quantum dots: tiny nanocrystals that emit pure, bright colors when exposed to light to enhance colors and brightness. Fancy tech aside, the results speak for themselves. The QM8L offers incredible brightness, far outshining its predecessor, the QM8K, alongside expansive colors that are as accurate as they are vibrant.

The new display offers other benefits, including fantastic black levels with very little light bleed, and reduced off-angle performance loss for most settings. Image processing has also improved, getting closer to the clarity and upscaling in top flagships from brands like LG and Samsung. The result is a premium picture that comes tantalizingly close to OLED displays in terms of contrast between the lightest and darkest images, and details that seem to pull you into the screen.

The TV’s Google TV interface is another plus, offering easy setup and extras like the ability to add albums from your Google Photos library as screen savers. Modern connectivity provides top-tier gaming features across inputs, and the sound isn’t bad either, thanks to built-in Bang & Olufsen speakers. Given that you can grab a 65-inch QM8L for as low as $1,000 or less on sale, it’s an easy pick for the best mini-LED TV available.

In a recent development, in many ways, entry-level TVs like the Hisense U6SF Pro are the best way to gauge how far TV tech has come in recent years. You just don’t expect a TV this cheap to look this good, from punchy brightness and naturalistic colors to minimal light bleed that lets you watch even challenging scenes in a dark room without being pulled out of the moment.

One sacrifice at this price is the TV’s black levels, which don’t look as rich as pricier mini-LED TVs, let alone self-lit OLED displays. Because of that, even though the TV’s brightness rises above anything you can stream, it can look less striking than step-up models. On the other hand, its matte-like screen does a great job of diminishing ambient light and even direct light reflections for a good picture day or night. That’s something I didn’t expect to see at this level.

You’ll get some handy features, including support for all major HDR formats and dual HDMI 2.1 ports with VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) up to 144 Hz for PC gaming, another impressive get at this price. I find the TV’s Fire TV smart system a little clunky, but it includes some cool extras, like Ambient Mode that displays free artwork. TCL’s QM6K is a good alternative thanks to its friendlier Google TV smart system, but it can’t match the U6SF Pro’s performance, which is the best I’ve tested at its price point.

The step-down model of our top-rated QM8L, TCL’s QM7L offers many of the same goodies that make its pricier sibling such a rock star, but at a much lower list price. It all starts with the same SQD display tech, for excellent brightness and color vibrancy, and the kind of dimensional contrast that pushes mini-LED closer to OLED.

In a recent development, the QM7L isn’t quite as much of a powerhouse as the QM8L, but it’s still put-on-your-sunglasses bright, blasting well past anything you can stream, and properly lighting high-quality 4K HDR Blu-rays. Its potency aids in remarkable color expansion for a deep dive into advanced films like Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse. Importantly, the TV also provides good color accuracy, along with deep black levels for excellent contrast. You’ll still see some minor light bleed if you look for it, and picture quality is reduced off-axis, but both are relatively minor concessions, especially for the price.

In a recent development, the TV offers a similarly loaded set of gaming features to last year’s QM7K, including options like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) and ALLM (Auto Low Latency Mode) across two of its four HDMI inputs. Like the QM8L, its Google TV smart system is intuitive to set up and use. That’s all icing on a TV that comes about as close as I’ve seen to a premium display for the money.

Industry observers note that hisense’s mid-tier mini-LED TV doesn’t offer the latest display technologies like RGB LED or Super Quantum Dots, but it does offer seriously punchy performance, along with a design that feels much more premium than its price class suggests. That starts with Hisense’s latest anti-reflective matte screen that eliminates most ambient reflections, matched by slim bezels and a stylish pedestal stand with the kind of build quality usually reserved for flagship TVs.

According to recent reports, under the hood is a potent mini-LED display that employs regular quantum dots for rich colors and brightness that meets or beats anything in its class, including TCL’s QM7L. When paired with its rich black levels and reflection-repelling screen, you’ll have no trouble watching even darker shows in a bright room. Hisense’s image processing has also improved for enhanced detail and upscaling with low-quality content. I did notice that the TV’s local dimming may create some artifacts at its highest setting, but it’s a very minor glitch. Like most backlit TVs, it also loses some picture quality when viewed from an angle.

Industry observers note that feature-wise, the U7SG is a gaming master, including VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 165 Hz across all four HDMI inputs, and handy extras like an intuitive game bar for adjusting settings on the fly. Add in its snappy Google TV interface, and you’re getting a whole lot of good stuff at a price that often falls well below $1,000 for a 65-inch model, and stays competitive up to a whopping 116 inches.

Sources indicate that after skipping a year, Hisense’s flagship U9 series is back, now loaded with the latest RGB LED display tech for a striking makeover. The TV uses its tri-colored red, green, and blue mini-LED backlighting to great effect, providing rich black levels and sparkling colors that increasingly close the gap with OLED, alongside the kind of dazzling brightness that OLED can’t yet match.

The UR9’s screen gets an advanced version of Hisense’s matte-like anti-glare coating called “Obsidian,” which impressively repels ambient and even most direct light sources, making it a great option in sunlit rooms. Turn the lights off, and you’ll find great shadow detail and very little light bleed from bright objects on dark backgrounds.

Sources indicate that hisense outfits the TV with some premium extras, from a capable 4.1.2-channel speaker system to HDMI 2.1 support at up to 165 Hz across all three HDMI inputs. There’s also a DisplayPort for connecting a PC, though I would have liked to see a fourth HDMI 2.1 port as well. The TV has also gotten an update for the latest advanced HDR format, Dolby Vision 2, making it well-primed for the future. It’s all wrapped in a stylish design, for a posh taste of next-gen luxury at an accessible price point.

In a recent development, TCL was so confident in its entry-level QM6K that it was the first TV the brand released with its fresh mini-LED display tech in 2025, and the only major model that wasn’t replaced for 2026. That badge of honor is well earned, as the QM6K is one of the best-performing TVs I’ve tested in its price class, with naturalistic colors, rich black levels and contrast, and enough brightness to properly light up HDR scenes like a blazing sunset or a jet’s afterburners.

Maybe just as impressive are the issues the QM6K avoids. While most TVs in its class readily reveal issues like screen aberrations on solid backgrounds, light bleed from bright images, and awful off-angle performance, the QM6K mostly stays clear of those pitfalls so you can simply enjoy the picture without distraction. My only real performance complaint is the TV’s particularly bad sound, but given that nearly all TVs I test are much better off with a soundbar or speaker system, that’s not a substantial surprise.

When it comes to extras, the QM6K is well stocked with options like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 144 Hz for blur-free action and a gaming bar to adjust features on the fly. And while the TV isn’t nearly as bright as my top budget pick, the U6SF Pro, its Google TV smart system is more intuitive and responsive for a better overall user experience. With a 55-inch model now available for under $500, the QM6K is tough to pass up.

In a recent development, most TVs on this list are available from 55 inches to large-scale models at 98 inches or larger, and at increasingly reasonable price points. A major reason for that is, unlike OLED, mini-LED TVs are scalable at a relatively low cost, so screens fit for large home theaters are much more attainable. That’s one of mini-LED’s biggest advantages over other display tech, not to mention the potential for next-gen brightness and color coverage at lower pricing. That stated, ultra-large screens more readily expose performance issues, so it’s key to balance screen size with quality so you don’t regret your purchase later.

Industry observers note that all of the TVs on this list offer 4K resolution with HDR (High Dynamic Range), and you wouldn’t want to buy a TV with lower resolution these days unless you’re looking for a very small screen (around 48 inches or lower) for a bedroom or office. The majority of latest content is shot in 4K with HDR, the latter of which provides higher brightness and better contrast between the lightest and darkest images, along with the potential for more vibrant colors. Some TVs still offer 8K resolution, but because 8K content is scarce and difficult to recognize with the naked eye, it’s essentially dead (or at least dormant) in the current TV landscape.

It has been revealed that as for refresh rates, any TV with 120-Hz or higher is preferred for fast-moving content like sports and, especially, gaming. All of the TVs on this list offer 120 Hz refresh rates or higher with VRR (Variable Refresh Rate), designed to adjust to games dynamically to reduce lag and screen tearing/blur. Many TVs push to 144 Hz or better, but those refresh rates are only accessible with select gaming PCs. For consoles—PS5, Xbox Series S/X, and the Nintendo Switch 2—120 Hz is sufficient.

All of the displays on this list use mini-LED-backlighting, a smaller and more accurate version of traditional LED backlighting, paired with a liquid-crystal display (LCD). Because mini-LEDs are smaller, they can be used more prevalently to create better brightness and more dimming zones, which can enhance black levels for better contrast between the brightest and darkest images. Mini-LEDs can also be enhanced by features like quantum dots, nanoparticles that produce pure bright colors when exposed to light. Some advanced Mini-LED TVs also use RGB LED technology, which trades uniform blue or white mini-LEDs for multicolor red, green, and blue light clusters designed to produce purer, more expansive colors at the light source.

Industry observers note that in contrast (no pun intended), OLED displays use organic material excited by electricity to light each of a TV’s millions of pixels independently. These self-lit (a.k.a. self-emissive) displays have distinct advantages, including the ability to create perfect black levels for enhanced contrast over backlit displays, along with much wider viewing angles. Like mini-LEDs, some OLED displays also use quantum dots: So-called “QD-OLED” TVs offer enhanced brightness and colors, among other new technologies to compete with ever-brighter and more advanced mini-LED TVs.

In a recent development, both display types have their advantages. OLED is the best choice for those after a more balanced, nuanced, and uniform picture, especially if money isn’t a concern. However, because mini-LED is generally cheaper to produce, it may be a better choice for those on a budget who want the largest and brightest screen for their money. And in recent years, the best mini-LED TVs have increasingly advanced to better compete against OLED.

According to recent reports, the most notable connectivity option for gamers is HDMI 2.1, which offers higher bandwidth to get the most out of gaming devices. HDMI 2.1 allows for high refresh rates and features like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) from devices like the PS5, Xbox Series X, and gaming PCs. If you’re only connecting a Blu-ray player or streaming device, HDMI 2.0 will suffice. All of the TVs on this list also support HDMI eARC/ARC, which allows you to easily connect newer soundbars and other audio devices at high resolution for enhanced audio performance.

Sources indicate that wiFi 6 or 7 may also be helpful for wireless streaming, especially if you’re watching a lot of high-resolution content, though you’ll need a router that supports those formats. Most TVs also include an Ethernet connection for a mainline connection to your modem. Other connection options to consider include Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, ATSC 3.0 for features like over-the-air HDR from an HD antenna, and an optical connection for older audio devices like a legacy amplifier or soundbar.

Sources indicate that all the TVs on this list come with a smart TV platform for streaming from popular apps, and many include options that let you stream content directly from a smartphone like Apple AirPlay or Google Cast. My favorite platforms are Roku and Google TV, which I find the easiest to navigate and use on a daily basis. All smart platforms collect some form of personal information, so it’s key to be careful when agreeing to terms and licensing to protect your privacy.

Sources indicate that each TV also supports multiple HDR formats, which is vital for getting the best performance. HDR10 is the baseline format, which all modern TVs support. Most TVs also support dynamic HDR formats like Dolby Vision and HDR10+ (many support both). These advanced formats can provide a more precise vision of a director’s intent by adjusting the brightest and darkest images scene by scene, and even frame by frame. Dolby Vision is the most common dynamic HDR format for streaming.

If you’re interested in voice control, you’ll want to look for voice assistants like Roku Voice, Amazon Alexa or Alexa+, and Google Assistant or Gemini. If you’re connecting an audio device that supports spatial audio, like a Dolby Atmos soundbar or A/V receiver, you may also want to ensure your TV supports 3D audio formats like Dolby Atmos and, for 4K Blu-rays, DTS:X.

Tech Report: ‘Political malpractice’: Calls grow to delay Senate GOP leadership elections

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1086 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer.
  • After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.
  • It has been revealed that “After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer. Now he’s pushing to delay leadership elections for his conference, urging a discussion of last week’s larger than expected losses. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.

It has been revealed that “After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual. That kind of defeat demands change,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., noted on Monday evening.

Industry observers note that asked if he himself would want to run for Senate minority leader, the Wisconsin Republican responded with a question of his own: “That’s part of our problem. Who’d want the job? Would you want it?”.

Though no hopeful had emerged as of Monday afternoon — at least publicly — to challenge current Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., for the top GOP post, the frustration was palpable as Republican senators returned to D.C. and grappled with the election results. Calls grew throughout the day to delay the conference’s leadership elections planned for Tuesday morning.

“Well, I mean, I’m open to hearing what the arguments are for that,” Thune told reporters Monday when asked about the possibility of postponing the leadership votes. “I don’t know if that solves anything, but like I stated, it’s going to be a decision that’s ultimately made by Republican senators. We’ll hear them out.”.

Johnson told reporters on Monday that if the election is held, he would “leave the room” and walk out. Either way, he seemed certain to at least get a “fulsome” discussion of the topic, as he requested in a letter he sent to Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Four other Republican senators signed on to the letter, hitting the threshold to call a conference meeting under internal GOP rules.

Recent findings suggest that also signed by Sens. Mike Lee of Utah, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida, and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter obtained by CQ Roll Call cites last week’s “stunning defeat” and reads in part: “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice.”.

Kennedy stated Monday evening that he was asking to postpone the leadership elections because “we need time to talk to each other.”.

“We’re like a shop owner who’s losing his customers. It’s not the customer’s job to fix that. It’s the shop owner’s job, and I’m not looking for blame-shifting. I’m looking for self-examination,” he remarked, adding that he wouldn’t consider running for minority leader himself.

In the letter, the group asked that at the time the leadership elections were set to begin, 9 a.m. on Tuesday, they instead “have a fulsome conference discussion and delay holding leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.”.

Thune echoed that wording Monday as he spoke to reporters, saying, “I do think that we need to have a very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here, and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”.

But Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who serves as chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, remarked she has seen such requests introduced in the past and didn’t think it would do much to affect the ultimate outcome. “I think Sen. Thune will be reelected,” she said.

Industry observers note that and several Senate GOP aides remarked that they suspected a “robust” conversation wouldn’t do much to delay the intends and that leadership elections were still expected to take place Tuesday. They noted similar efforts from some of those same senators in previous years to sow discord in the ranks.

According to recent reports, that includes Scott, who unsuccessfully challenged Thune in 2024 and then-GOP leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022. But Scott told Fox News over the weekend, “I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice.”.

Republicans “failed. We had a horrible night,” Scott mentioned. “Instead of having an [leadership] election, the first thing you do is you say, ‘OK, what are we going to change? We have to change something.’”.

Lee floated the idea of waiting until after the uncalled Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska are officially resolved.

In a recent development, an online pressure campaign was building in some of the same MAGA corners of the internet that have pushed to pass a sweeping voter ID bill, known as the SAVE America Act, that has stalled in the Senate. On Monday morning, influencer Scott Presler in an X post urged constituents to call their senators while praising the lawmakers who have already pushed for the leadership elections to be postponed. “Where is everyone else?” he wrote.

Sens. Jim Banks of Indiana and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania also called for a delay, though they did not appear on Johnson’s letter.

In a recent development, “A week ago, we had the worst election results in decades,” McCormick said in a post on X, calling Tuesday “too soon” to vote for leaders. “I know it’s been practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it.”.

Banks similarly remarked Tuesday was “too soon,” posting on social media, “Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here.”.

Industry observers note that one senator speaking out in Thune’s defense was Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who competed with Thune for the top spot in 2024 but on Monday said the leader isn’t to blame for the midterm results.

“I think the president needs to look in the mirror and look at the flawed candidates that he endorsed, and the kind of environment that we’re in,” stated Cornyn, who is still smarting from losing his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump.

It has been revealed that cornyn’s loss means he has no say in the coming conference leadership elections. But he said, “I think Thune’s a good man, and did as well as he could against a president and an environment that was pretty hostile.”.

Industry News: Do You Trust Your Own Intuition? Here’s How You Sharpen It—And Win at Life, Researchers Say

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • It has been revealed that think about the phrase “it’s just like riding a bicycle.” At first, it’s hard, and you have to pay attention to what you’re doing, but after you’ve practiced for many hours, bike riding becomes so natural you don’t even have to think about it; you just hop on and go.
  • Intuition is about finding the solution automatically and without deep thought, indicates Wim De Neys, a cognitive psychologist and CNRS research professor at the University of Paris.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

It has been revealed that think about the phrase “it’s just like riding a bicycle.” At first, it’s hard, and you have to pay attention to what you’re doing, but after you’ve practiced for many hours, bike riding becomes so natural you don’t even have to think about it; you just hop on and go. In fact, you can hardly explain how you learned in the first place or exactly how you’re keeping your balance as you pedal on. You just trust your body to do it. The same applies to cognitive activities: As a child, you had to really think about how to arrive at the answer of 2+2, but now, you just know it’s four, without thinking.

Intuition is about finding the solution automatically and without deep thought, indicates Wim De Neys, a cognitive psychologist and CNRS research professor at the University of Paris. At its core, your intuition is a behavior your brain develops based on patterns and experiences over time, a kind of automation for something you’ve done countless times. That’s why intuition is often linked to expertise. Trusting your gut may sound ill-advised, so why wouldn’t you want to think things through? But it turns out that generating your instincts for decision-making can both help you make the right choice in times of confusion and stress, and also free up mental resources for other tasks.

So, can you train your intuition to sense better choices?

In a recent development, well, it’s not that simple, according to De Neys, whose research focuses on how intuitive and deliberate thinking develops over our lifetimes. You can’t sidestep the deep reflection needed to build the foundation of your intuitions. But you can tap into them in a more meaningful way, especially over time.

Recent findings suggest that “Having gut feelings and intuition and even valid intuitions, there’s science to back it up,” De Neys claims. “It exists, but it’s always tied to expertise, and expertise means it’s something that you’ve done a lot.”.

Sources indicate that intuition isn’t some overall sense; instead it’s tied to one area of expertise, like an interviewer being able to pick up on the candidate who’ll be the right fit for the job, or an experienced doctor delivering a diagnosis. While you won’t have expert intuition about everything under the sun, there are a few ways you can boost your own decision-making.

First, you need to get better at pattern matching, and that means practice. Intuition is tied to pattern-matching, Jeff Larsen, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains. For example, chess masters earn their distinction by practicing so much that when they see the board, they don’t have to stop and think about what the two or three best moves will be. Others with less expertise may watch a game and think, “that was a silly move,” but they don’t realize the master player has spent years building up pattern recognition, or an accurate gut feeling, Larsen explains.

In a recent development, second, stop second-guessing your intuition. You can do this by asking yourself, “How might I be wrong?” One approach is to ask a friend who may disagree with you or might have an outside perspective. This can also help you understand that, often, an instinctual choice you made in the heat of the moment is correct. Even if the choice isn’t exactly right, it’s probably good enough to keep you safe. For example, when you’re driving down the interstate, you have some intuition about whether you can make a lane change or not, and whether you need to slow down or speed up to avoid an accident. Thinking about the consequences of your decision-making can also help give you more confidence in your intuition.

Sometimes you have to trust your gut on a truly life-changing decision. When it comes to marriage, the information overload can sometimes feel overwhelming. However, when it comes to close relationships, you’ve presumably experienced many behavioral exchanges with your partner, and this allows for substantial information-gathering to “feed your gut,” Michael Olson, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains.

Since you can’t possibly keep this massive load of information in your conscious memory at all times, it translates into a neat summary of all those behavioral exchanges. Now you have a gut feeling that this person is right for you—or not.

And the research agrees. A study Olson coauthored, published in Science, found that the “explicit,” or “conscious” evaluations couples in the study made of their partners while in the so-called initial “honeymoon stage” didn’t mean as much when stretched over four years. Instead, those who reported positive gut feelings over this time period had a more accurate idea of their happiness in their relationship.

Your gut doesn’t just extend to your love life. Trusting it can also help you to be successful in business. Elizabeth Rea, an evidentiary clairvoyant psychic medium, now teaches established founders and CEOs to tap into their own intuitions, through her company, Insightful. As a medium, Rea has also assisted U.S. federal special agents investigating cold murder cases.

In a recent development, when working with clients, she asks them to relax what they consciously believe. Sometimes so-called gut feelings may come to us in the form of chills down our spine or another physical sensation. But since we’re living in a left-brained culture that prizes making decisions using logic and analysis, those instincts often get passed off as coincidences and ignored, Rea says. Sometimes, gut feelings may also be ignored because of self-doubt. Your intuition often whispers to you, she tells clients. Honing these signals will help you improve your self-trust—thereby improving your intuition.

Recent findings suggest that overall, training yourself to trust your intuition will help you become a better decision-maker. You’ll make the right choices without the agonizing process of picking through pros and cons and running scenarios in your brain for days on end.

According to recent reports, “It’s a lot more cost-efficient if we can offload [decision-making] to our intuition,” De Neys states. “Often that’s going to be helpful because then it frees up resources for something else that might be more important at that point in time.”.
