  • Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.
  • Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov. 10. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

“I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune said of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

Industry observers note that sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

“They got to give us an upgrade,” Tillis remarked. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”.

Sources indicate that sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly stated legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

According to recent reports, duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who said over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

Sources indicate that the White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration remarked Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy remarked the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

“In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand new architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy mentioned on CNBC Monday. “This can happen quickly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”.

In a recent development, A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he remarked included “some other stuff” as well.

Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”.

The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

Thune said Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the new request specifically for air traffic control related challenges, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

“I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune said. “We’ll hear him out.”.

Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the latest funding request.

Sources indicate that “So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., mentioned on the floor.

Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

Industry observers note that passengers aboard American Airlines flight 2609 from Miami (MIA) to Atlanta (ATL) on November 16, 2026, reported an unpleasant surprise at baggage claim. Travelers waited more than two hours before their luggage appeared on carousel eight at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport. When the bags arrived, passengers saw a brown substance smeared across them and naturally feared the worst.

(my mind goes to Diddy Combs and AstroGlide…).

Recent findings suggest that american later mentioned that liquefied peanut butter had leaked from a passenger’s checked bag, affecting nearby luggage. The airline said an environmental inspection confirmed its explanation.

“Unfortunately, a food item from a customer’s checked bag leaked during the flight, affecting several bags nearby.”.

In a recent development, I would certainly prefer peanut butter to the alternative passengers feared. But I would still be rather unhappy about finding someone else’s sandwich spread having spoiled my suitcase.

It isn’t clear how much peanut butter was involved, how it was packaged, or exactly how it spread…feel free to speculate.

Even if you carefully pack your own suitcase, you have no control over what someone else puts in theirs. While that’s true in a shared overhead bin too, it’s much less likely to be a problem.

There is some dark humor in a baggage carousel full of passengers trying to determine whether what that brown stuff was all over their bag, but I’m sure there was nothing to laugh about if that was your bag covered in brown.

American Airlines notes peanut butter leaking from a checked bag caused the brown mess passengers discovered on their luggage in Atlanta. Industry News: No more permanent coalitions: What the midterm results reveal

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (903 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 9 for a group photo with incoming members of his caucus: from left, Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Texas' James Talarico, Iowa's Josh Turek, Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, North Carolina's Roy Cooper, Illinois' Juliana Stratton, New Hampshire's Chris Pappas, South Carolina's Annie Andrews, Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, Maine's Troy Jackson and Kansas' Adam Hamilton.
  • Industry observers note that ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once said.
  • In 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer poses in his office on Nov. 9 for a group photo with incoming members of his caucus: from left, Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Texas' James Talarico, Iowa's Josh Turek, Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, North Carolina's Roy Cooper, Illinois' Juliana Stratton, New Hampshire's Chris Pappas, South Carolina's Annie Andrews, Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, Maine's Troy Jackson and Kansas' Adam Hamilton. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

Industry observers note that ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once said. “If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”.

In 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness. Republicans had captured the White House, flipped the Senate and held the House. President Donald Trump had completely altered the party coalitions as he led the ascendant GOP to victory.

Now, just two years later, Democrats are on the rise. A historic midterm tsunami has swept them into such commanding Senate and House majorities that some are questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again. And if Texas is blue, how does the GOP have any chance in the Electoral College again?

A significant takeaway from the midterm results should be that there’s very little permanence in our politics.

What may have looked like a new GOP coalition was really more of a Trump coalition, and it crumbled in the face of economic frustrations, affordability concerns and the president’s unpopular policies.

With Trump’s negative job approval rating weighing them down, Republican candidates suffered losses among virtually all demographic groups – including by wide margins among constituencies thought to make up the GOP’s core.

It has been revealed that trump or the Republicans finished ahead among male voters by 4 points in 2018, 8 points in 2020, 14 points in 2022 and 12 points in 2024, according to the exit polls. Men went for Democratic candidates by 4 points (51 percent to 47 percent) this cycle. Meanwhile, Republicans lost even more ground among women. While Kamala Harris finished ahead of Trump by 8 points in 2024, that margin grew to 21 points for Democratic candidates this year.

Trump closed the gap among Hispanic voters to just 5 points behind Harris two years ago. This year, Hispanic voters nationwide supported Democratic candidates by 32 points (65 percent to 33 percent). Even white voters shifted significantly. They backed Trump or  Republican candidates by 10 points in 2018, 17 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022 and 15 points in 2024. And yet Democrats edged out Republicans by a point (50 percent to 49 percent) on Nov. 3.

Voters without a college degree were supposed to be a key cog in Republicans’ latest populist coalition. But they went from +13 (56 percent to 43 percent) for Trump in 2024 to backing Republican candidates by just 1 point this year. Meanwhile, the gap among voters with a college degree went from 14 points for Harris in 2024 to 30 points for Democrats this cycle.

According to recent reports, republicans had closed the gap among young voters aged 18 to 29 from 35 points in 2018 to just 11 points in 2024. But younger voters supported Democratic candidates this year by 50 points (74 percent to 24 percent). Not to mention Democrats flipped voters aged 45 to 64 for the first time in nearly two decades.

In a recent development, white evangelicals appear to be one of the only groups that didn’t shift toward Democrats. They supported GOP candidates 82 percent to 17 percent. But they only made up 17 percent of the electorate, according to the exit polls, which is down from a very consistent 25 percent for more than a decade. So there was still a problem with that group of voters, but it was more about turnout than persuasion.

While there was an unmistakable leftward shift this year, the results should not be considered a permanent party realignment any more than 2024 was. While Democrats did extremely well in Texas this year, they still haven’t won the Lone Star State in a presidential race in 50 years. So maybe it’s wise for everyone to take a deep breath.

If you take this year’s election results and match them with the Senate seats on the ballot in 2028, there doesn’t appear to be a viable path for Republicans back to the majority. But there wasn’t a particularly viable Democratic path to the Senate majority at this point two years ago. And if the Alaska election goes their way, they will end up winning Senate races in seven states that were initially rated Solid Republican.

If one party starts to get too comfortable, voters have a way of bringing politicians back down to earth. If Democrats come to Congress and push too far to the left or become too defined by their most extreme members, they will squander the opportunity they earned this year.

The dramatic demographic swings should be evidence that many voters are not beholden to either party and are open to switching allegiances, particularly in a time of economic uncertainty.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, if Republicans don’t go through some time of reflection and instead triple down on the policies that led to the blue wave, they risk cementing some of the shifts that started this cycle. It just won’t be thick cement.

According to a recent memo to flight attendants, United is gradually reintroducing Sprite Winter Spiced Cranberry during November, with availability continuing through December.

The Sleigh Bell Spritz features:.

According to recent reports, the cocktail costs $10 in United Economy and is complimentary in premium cabins. United also mentioned the returning drink in its recent Thanksgiving travel announcement, suggesting a squeeze of lime alongside the vodka, seasonal Sprite, and fresh cranberries.

According to recent reports, the internal memo says hub catering locations will supply cranberries for both United First and economy service. I’m not a fan of Sprite (far too sweet), but may try one…for the blog of course.

The Sleigh Bell Spritz is returning to United Airlines through December, with a gradual rollout during November and a $10 price in economy. If you are flying United over the Christmas holidays and looking for something a bit different to drink, there’s your opportunity.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My trip to New York on Air France began with a short domestic flight on the Embraer 170 in business class from Basel to Paris, a short and pleasant journey.

Years ago after my La Premiere flight from Los Angeles to Paris, I continued on to Basel on an Embraer 190 in what Air France marketed as business class. But the service onboard was no different than economy class: there was no blocked middle seat, meal, or beverages served in glass..it was just regular economy class service.

But Air France has come a long way and I feel like even on a short domestic business class flight it really has really raised the bar in terms of service.

I booked my ticket from Basel to New York JFK via Paris for 60,000 Flying Blue miles and $453 in business class, booking just 36 hours prior to departure (so yes, Air France does release last-minute award space).

It has been revealed that basel Airport straddles Switzerland and France. I entered on the French side and checked in for my flight.

Sources indicate that on the check-in level you can walk back and forth freely between the French and Swiss side, but on the lower level and upper level there’s a physical barrier. For example, I went out to the terrace on the upper level and there’s a fence separating the two nations.

After visiting the Skyview Lounge, now operated by Aspire, I headed to the gate for boarding at 1:45 pm, which began right on schedule.

Stepping onboard, I found my seat in 2F.

Recent findings suggest that the aircraft has 76 seats in a 2-2 configuration. Each seat has 31 inches of pitch and is 18 inches wide. Seats recline three inches. There are individual air vents, but no power of any kind: neither USB or a universal power socket.

Business class can be adjusted according to demand, the “genius” of having the same seat. On today’s flight there were three rows of business class, but only three passengers: we each had our own row. Air France now blocks adjacent seats in business class, so that is a big advantage versus economy class.

The only other business class distinctive was that each seat had a pillow and water bottle:.

At only 250 miles, there wasn’t  much time for a meal service.

Recent findings suggest that air France nevertheless offers business class passengers a small meal box on its shorthaul network, part of a catering concept introduced in 2024 and developed with Servair Corporate Chef François Adamski, a Bocuse d’Or winner and Meilleur Ouvrier de France. For flights departing after 10:00 am, Air France serves what it calls a “signature” sandwich along with a French sweet or dessert, with the selection changing regularly. It is served in a sturdy cardboard box.

On my flight, the meal consisted of two finger sandwiches with smoked salmon and a creamy herb filling on brown bread, along with a small pecan tart and a chocolate…a very nice treat. The airline also serves wine and Champagne in proper glassware, though I just had sparkling water on this flight.

> Read More: Air France Served This Surprisingly Elegant Business Class Meal On A 250-Mile Flight.

Flight attendants onboard were very polite and efficient: meals and drinks were offered immediately and refills offered after they had completed service in economy class and again before landing, all on a very short flight.

This flight has no internet and no in-flight-entertainment, but Starlink is coming to these jets.

However, it was a beautiful day tempearture wise and I enjoyed looking out the window, especially as we flew over Paris (thought it was a bit hazy) as we neared CDG.

Business class passengers have a dedicated lavatory in the font of the cabin. It was small but clean.

We landed on time in Paris where I ran into a fairly complicated connection to Terminal 2E Hall M…but it was a short but lovely flight.

TAP Air Portugal will launch a latest route to Washington, D.C., next year.

Recent findings suggest that starting March 30, 2027, the carrier will connect Porto and Washington Dulles. Flights will operate three times weekly.

Currently, TAP serves Dulles from its hub at Humberto Delgado Airport in Lisbon. Its only U.S.-bound routes from Porto are to Boston and Newark, New Jersey.

TAP officials said the fresh connection will strengthen the airline’s presence in northern Portugal while expanding access to a vital foreign market.

TAP serves Porto via Francisco Sá Carneiro Airport.

The carrier serves nine destinations in the U.S., the others being New York-JFK, Chicago O’Hare, Orlando, Florida, Miami, Los Angeles, and San Francisco.

  • Finnair marked International Men’s Day with an all-male crew on a flight from Helsinki to London, drawing attention to how few men work as flight attendants at the airline.
  • On November 19, 2026, Finnair operated flight AY1331 from Helsinki (HEL) to London Heathrow (LHR) with an all-male crew aboard an Airbus A350-900.
  • As noted by Ben from One Mile At A Time, Finnair states only about 10% of its cabin crew are male and would like that proportion to grow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finnair marked International Men’s Day with an all-male crew on a flight from Helsinki to London, drawing attention to how few men work as flight attendants at the airline. Encouraging women to become pilots and encouraging men to become flight attendants strike me as entirely consistent goals.

On November 19, 2026, Finnair operated flight AY1331 from Helsinki (HEL) to London Heathrow (LHR) with an all-male crew aboard an Airbus A350-900. The crew included two pilots and eight flight attendants. The gate agents were also men.

As noted by Ben from One Mile At A Time, Finnair states only about 10% of its cabin crew are male and would like that proportion to grow.

I have flown Finnair many times and cannot recall ever having a male flight attendant. That is very different from my experience on virtually any other European carrier I regularly fly. My sample size is hardly enormous, but the statistic helps explain why this initiative caught my attention.

Ben also addresses an interesting paradox at certain airlines, singling out IndiGo.

Sources indicate that the Indian carrier has good reason to celebrate its female pilots. In March, IndiGo announced that it had more than 1,000 women pilots, representing 17.5% of its pilot workforce. Yet its published entry-level cabin attendant eligibility criteria specify:.

“Female Indian nationals, with Indian passport, between 18 to 27 years of age.”.

That is an explicit restriction in the recruitment criteria, rather than simply a workforce in which women happen to predominate.

The nationality requirement is a separate question from the gender restriction. But the latter creates an odd contrast: women are encouraged to pursue a career historically associated with men in the cockpit, while men are excluded from this advertised path into the cabin.

I agree with Ben that a boy who grows up wanting to become a flight attendant should be able to pursue that ambition, just as a girl who wants to become a pilot should. No, that does not mean every airline needs a precisely equal number of male and female employees in every role. Different people will make different career choices. But there is a considerable difference between who chooses to apply and who is allowed to apply.

Flight attendants are primarily present for passenger safety, yet that does not make their hospitality role unimportant…I do not object to airlines making a polished cabin crew part of their brand.

For example, I have no inherent problem with the glamour associated with the “Singapore Girl.” An airline can take pride in elegant uniforms and gracious service while ensuring its crew are trained and respected as safety professionals.

But none of that establishes that hospitality is exclusively a female vocation. Singapore Airlines employs male cabin crew too.

It has been revealed that I have been an usher at my church for 20 years, and I love that volunteer work. There is something deeply gratifying about welcoming people and helping them feel comfortable, including those who may be visiting for the first time.

In a recent development, I am not equating passing out service leaflets or collecting offerings with managing an aircraft evacuation! But there is an element of hospitality common to both roles, and I enjoy it. Men can—and should—be hospitable too. There is nothing inherently feminine about taking good care of another person.

Industry observers note that if you have seen On the Basis of Sex, you may remember the case involving Charles Moritz, a never-married man who was denied a tax deduction for expenses incurred caring for his elderly mother. Ruth Bader Ginsburg and her husband, Martin, represented him. The law allowed the deduction for women and certain categories of men, but excluded a man in his circumstances.

According to recent reports, in Moritz v. Commissioner, the Tenth Circuit ruled in his favor in 1972.

I cannot oversimplify by suggesting American sex-discrimination protections began with male plaintiffs. Ginsburg also helped secure the 1971 victory in Reed v. Reed, involving discrimination against a woman. But representing men disadvantaged by sex-based rules was an notable part of her strategy. It helped demonstrate that assumptions about the proper roles of men and women could harm both.

Ginsburg later discussed that litigation strategy, including the challenge of persuading judges and legislators who often viewed different treatment as protective of women. I find the principle relevant here. A rule premised on women being caregivers can disadvantage a man caring for his mother. A rule treating hospitality as women’s work can exclude a man perfectly capable of providing excellent service and can reasonably run afoul of public policy.

Removing those restrictions benefits people who do not fit the stereotype, whichever sex they happen to be.

An all-male Finnair flight is a small gesture, but one with a sensible purpose when men account for only about 10% of its cabin crew.

I welcome efforts to show people that an aviation career is open to them, whether that means a woman becoming a captain or a man becoming a flight attendant. I enjoy the elegance and hospitality that airlines can bring to flying. I simply see no reason qualified men should be excluded from providing it.

“This is so nervewracking,” she said, before pulling out a chip with a “1” printed on it.

Her prize was a coveted one — first choice of office space. Every two years, incoming members of the House play a game of chance to see who can land the best real estate and who will be relegated to less desirable corners of the Capitol complex.

In a recent development, the room broke out in raucous applause and a standing ovation. Her new colleagues started singing “Happy Birthday.”.

“Lets all hope for the luck of the Taylors,” mentioned Rep.-elect Brent Taylor, R-Tenn., only to emerge with number 81.

The newly-elected members got their turn in a random order, walking up one by one to a table where deputy executive director of House Office Buildings Kornell Rancy kept watch over the box of chips.

Sources indicate that rep.-elect John Cowan, R-Ga., was the first to pick a number. The first neurosurgeon to be elected to Congress, Cowan wore his white doctor’s coat as he pulled number 11 out of the box.

“I wanted to do something where I’m just representing health care providers around the country,” Cowan said.

Industry observers note that as returning members lay claim to more desirable offices made available by those who resign, retire or lose elections, the space they’ve abandoned is left for the newcomers, who are on the Hill this week for orientation. Industry observers note that not all offices are created equal, and the calculus has changed over the years. The previously undesirable Cannon Building just underwent a budget-busting renovation that lasted more than a decade, with a spacious courtyard opening earlier this year. But the coveted Rayburn Building still retains its prestige, despite repeated and dire warnings from the Architect of the Capitol about its crumbling infrastructure.

“You’re welcome,” said Rep.-elect Amish Shah, D-Ariz., after pulling a disappointing number 94.

It has been revealed that “If I don’t pick number one, I’m going to offer one of these cigars as a trade to whoever gets it,” he said, pointing to three of them sticking out of his jacket pocket. He’s preparing to take over the seat presently held by his twin brother Troy, who shares a fondness for stogies.

It has been revealed that the office space lottery dates back to 1908, when members of the 60th Congress received their first office assignments after the completion of what would be named the Cannon Building. A House page drew names and numbers from a box, and members selected their offices from a chart, according to House Office Buildings executive director of facility operations Joe Yates, who kicked things off Tuesday with a history lesson.

The lottery now is a little more modern, with members poring over virtual office layouts and doing walkthroughs of spaces on laptops.

And when Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., the last of the incoming members to draw, walked up to the table, the whole room cheered.

“Wouldn’t it be crazy if I picked number 1?” he joked, pulling out the last chip in the box.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, united Airlines CEO Scott Kirby thanked employees for helping passengers through the nationwide FAA disruption, singling out a crew that helped a mother with three tired children through the airport. But his message also included a striking assessment of the crisis: it was “nobody’s fault,” and the private sector needs a greater role in fixing the system. I appreciate his focus on solutions, though that does not eliminate the need for accountability.

In a video message to United employees reviewed by Live And Let’s Fly, Kirby praised the airline’s recovery from the FAA ground stop and described conversations with administration officials and congressional leaders from both parties.

Industry observers note that he argued that fixing air traffic control requires more than money and asked for private-sector involvement in the process. But he began with the people who took care of passengers during the disruption, including the crew pictured above.

Here is the full transcript of his remarks:.

Hello everyone, I wanted to come to you today before the holidays and say thank you for the amazing job that you did, taking care of each other and our customers during the FAA shut down over the past weekend. You really did do an amazing job. If I look at the numbers, our airline recovered better than any of our large competitors. If I look at the NPS scores, remarkable how positive they were because all of you were really committed to taking care of customers.

While I can look at the numbers, the anecdotes meant even more to me: the customers that I heard from, all the special things that our people, that all of you, did for customers really helped build the brand and really made all of us shine in a moment of difficulty. My favorite, perhaps, was that picture of the crew helping a mother with three young children get through the airport when they were tired and they were sleepy, and it hit two of the things that are really crucial to me: build an airline that is great for customers, and I think of that is make it easy for parents with young children to travel, but also an airline where our people committed to doing the right thing and taking care of customers.

So thank you for all that you did working hard over the weekend and while you were working hard taking care of customers, I was busy on the phone talking to people in the administration, the leadership on both sides of the aisle in both the House and the Senate to really try to get this fixed.

According to recent reports, so I’m not going to play the blame game because this has been building for decades. And the truth is this is nobody’s fault, but it is everybody’s responsibility to fix it. And it’s not just about money. It’s going to be about having a real process and having a real engagement to fix it. My request, frankly, is to let us be inside the tent. Let the private sector, we know how to do some of this stuff. We care about it more than anyone, for you and for our customers. And so I am committed, and I got great commitments from people on both sides of the aisle. Everyone wants to fix this but we need to stop talking about it and finally get it over the finish line.

Recent findings suggest that so thank you for all that you did to work really hard taking care of customers. Thank you for the best recovery of anyone in the industry. Thank you in advance for all you’re gonna do to take care of customers over the busy holiday travel that’s about to come up on us, so thank you. I’ll see you in the friendly skies.

The photo Kirby referenced is my favorite part of this message too.

According to recent reports, according to his account, the crew was helping a mother traveling with three young children. You can see crew members carrying children while others pull luggage through the terminal. Here’s the original Instagram post:.

A post shared by Tammy Stull (@thetammystull).

As a father who has traveled extensively with young children, I recognize how valuable an extra pair of hands can be!

According to recent reports, after a long delay, even the walk out of the airport can feel daunting (remember this?). A child falls asleep, another needs attention, and the bags (all of them) must carried. Someone stepping in to help can change how you remember the entire day.

Kirby talks about building the United brand through those encounters. That is certainly true and I really like that he recognized this particular act of kindness in a message to the broader workforce. Employees should hear that helping a tired family is a core mission of the job and that employees are already stepping up in a beautiful way.

In a recent development, his claims about United having the best recovery and positive Net Promoter Scores are his assessment. That could be a classic Kirby exaggeration, but having flown last weekend myself, everyone seemed to be in a good mood despite a delayed departure.

It has been revealed that I agree that America’s air traffic control problems have developed over decades. I also agree that another round of partisan finger-pointing will not modernize the system and in some ways is just not constructive.

But I cannot agree with the blanket assertion that this is nobody’s fault. There are two different problems here: the longstanding condition of the infrastructure and the decisions surrounding the work that preceded this particular disruption.

It has been revealed that as I discussed yesterday, newly introduced reporting raises questions about contractor supervision and changes to the FAA’s maintenance approval process. Those questions still require answers.

Industry observers note that I take Kirby’s point to be that everyone should stop using the crisis to attack political opponents and start working together. That is a worthwhile appeal and one that I share. But identifying responsibility is part of preventing another failure.

In a recent development, if an oversight process was inadequate, it needs to change. If a contractor failed to follow required procedures, that needs to be addressed, no matter how often its work went smoothly in the past. If the agency lacked sufficient staff or technical expertise, the remedy should reflect that. We cannot reliably fix a problem while declaring in advance that nobody bears responsibility for it…but I’ll stop beating a dead horse.

According to recent reports, kirby’s request for private-sector involvement is bold, but far too generalized to give us insight into the seriousness of that wish. Airlines have a direct interest in a functioning air traffic control system. Disruptions strand their aircraft and crews, cost them money, and leave their employees dealing with understandably frustrated passengers. Their operational experience should inform the modernization effort.

In a recent development, but Kirby did not describe a specific governance proposal in this message. Asking to be involved does not, by itself, amount to a detailed plan for privatization or airline control of air traffic services. I would want to see what he proposes before endorsing or rejecting it…and wonder what it is that United or other carriers can bring to the table that would actually help the FAA.

There is also an obvious complication: a private contractor was already involved in the work at the center of this disruption. Private-sector participation alone does not guarantee competent execution any more than government involvement guarantees failure.

Kirby’s observation that this is not just about money is very true. New equipment requires funding. So do the people needed to install, maintain, and supervise it. But an appropriation cannot substitute for a sound implementation and oversight process.

Recent findings suggest that I also appreciate he is holding conversations with leaders from both parties. That is the work airline executives should be doing when a problem this consequential affects their customers and employees…he has to be friends with everyone in the impending era of divided government.

I made a similar point yesterday: Congress needs to investigate what happened while working with the administration on practical improvements. We do not need to choose between accountability and cooperation…let’s just get it done.

Kirby can use his access to help advance that work. I hope he does.

Kirby’s message combines well-deserved recognition for employees with an appeal to stop arguing and fix air traffic control.

According to recent reports, the crew helping a mother with tired children deserves the praise. His call for a serious process, rather than simply another demand for money, is true, but I liken it to a political talking point and working together should begin with an honest accounting of what failed. A willingness to cooperate is valuable: so is a willingness to accept responsibility.

In the meantime, that photograph is a welcome reminder that employees can still take excellent care of people during a deeply frustrating travel day. Kudos to those employees for practically showing, “Good Leads The Way.“.

According to recent reports, kentucky Rep. James Comer, here talking to reporters on Capitol Hill in June, is running for governor. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Industry observers note that kentucky Rep. James R. Comer, whose role as chairman of the House Oversight Committee gave him a powerful platform to investigate Democrats, including former Presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, has released a run for governor next year.

The Republican, who was just elected to a sixth full term representing Kentucky’s 1st District, is seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. Kentucky is one of three states holding off-year gubernatorial elections in 2027, alongside Louisiana and Mississippi.

In his announcement at a tele-town hall Monday night, Comey emphasized pocketbook complications, pledging to eliminate the state income tax and boost job-creation in Louisville.

“If we get that income tax to zero, people are going to have more money to spend, and we're going to be able to attract more good-paying jobs to Kentucky, which will be able to keep our best and brightest in the state,’’ he noted.

In a recent development, as the leader of the House Oversight panel, Comer has been at the forefront in the fight over the release of records related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. (Last week, the committee released a report concluding that the federal government mishandled criminal probes into Epstein’s activities.).

Comer is a staunch ally of President Donald Trump, who carried Kentucky by 31 points in 2024, and his hard-nosed style of politics is conveyed in a soft-spoken Southern drawl.

Sources indicate that known back home as Jamie, Comer has deep roots in rural Monroe County, dating back to the late 1700s. Prior to coming to Congress, he operated a farm before serving 11 years in the Kentucky House. In 2011, he was elected as the commonwealth’s commissioner of agriculture.

He made an unsuccessful run for governor in 2015, losing the Republican primary by 83 votes to Matt Bevin, who went on to win the general election. The following year, Comer easily won election to the House from his western Kentucky district, succeeding Republican Ed Whitfield.

Recent findings suggest that comer has moved promptly to consolidate GOP support for his gubernatorial bid. He already has the backing of Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul and Sen.-elect Andy Barr. Michael Adams, Kentucky’s term-limited secretary of state who’d been seen a potential contender, gave Comer an early endorsement this summer.

Recent findings suggest that while Comer enters the race as the Republican front-runner, he won’t have the field to himself. Other declared hopefuls include local prosecutor Rick Hardin and distiller Charles “Bruiser” Martin, who appeared on the Discovery Channel show “Moonshiners: Master Distiller.”.

Recent findings suggest that while Kentucky has in recent decades grown reliably Republican at the federal level, the GOP has won just two gubernatorial elections there over the past half century. Two high-profile Democrats have already debuted bids to keep the governor’s mansion in party hands: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former state House Majority Leader and Beshear adviser Rocky Adkins, who ran for governor in 2019.

In a statement Tuesday, the Democratic Governors Association dismissed Comer as “a job-killing, pro-war politician who looks down on everyday Kentuckians.”.

  • Cruises can be affordable, but costs can rise quickly if you’re not strategic with booking and onboard spending.

    • In a recent development, the campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads.
    • However, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov. 11. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images).

    In a recent development, the campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads. The “pick another protein” spot will forever be stuck in the brains of a huge swath of Americans, especially Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. She underestimated Colom and his team, and will soon be an ex-senator.

    However, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

    The ad delivered an all-American lesson about history, born of bravery and sacrifice.

    Filmed at the Jackson, Miss., home of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, the ad featured Colom recounting the story of Evers, a World War II veteran who survived Normandy, only to be shot in the back by a racist assassin, resentful that a Black man dared to exercise his rights as a citizen in the country he fought for.

    Recent findings suggest that “He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”.

    In a state where voting is still racially polarized, it was clear that Colom would not win over a majority of white voters; he won an estimated 25 percent, better than Democrats in recent elections and cutting into Trump’s margins, but certainly not a path to victory.

    Recent findings suggest that black voters in Mississippi made the difference, as they often have. With their allies in the cause of justice, they heeded the call. They showed up despite the state’s stringent and often confusing voting restrictions, purges of the voting rolls engineered by Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson (who used unverified data from a credit bureau), and the U.S. Supreme Court Louisiana v. Callais decision that led to a wave of Southern states breaking up Black-majority districts.

    When the Mississippi purges resulted in “affidavit ballots” that required verification to count, as The Washington Post reported, young Black women tracked down those voters, one by one, to do everything they could to ensure voters’ efforts were not in vain.

    Black voters mattered in states all over the country, but especially in the South, where low turnout has plagued Democrats, particularly in midterm elections.

    Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected the first Black female governor in the country in Georgia, where Democrats won up and down the ballot. Newly elected senators Annie Andrews in South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas campaigned for and earned support from Black voters with proposals that rose above platitudes. And don’t sleep on North Carolina, where voters flipped seats the GOP tried to gerrymander into a hardened majority. The sight of hundreds of students from HBCU NC A&T State University, denied a campus early voting site, marching to the polls, must have made the ancestors smile.

    In Florida and Louisiana, where Democrats had little financial support and lost their statewide races, Black voters brought them tantalizingly close to victory and energized for the contests to come.

    Industry observers note that I still don’t expect Republicans to give up the election shenanigans, done in the name of “election integrity” and color blindness but in reality designed to demoralize as much as suppress. Why try to win over a diverse electorate with an inclusive, policy-driven message when manipulating Black-majority districts can still work?

    It has been revealed that the number of Black U.S. House members in the next session of Congress will fall, offset by a few Democrats who survived in redrawn districts, including Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina.

    But you can’t redistrict a state, and you can’t skip town halls and expect tradition, support for the Confederacy and an “R” after your name to forever save you — the Hyde-Smith playbook.

    "I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator," she bragged, too soon, on election night.

    Maybe she should have emphasized affordability, saving rural hospitals and serving all Mississippians, as Colom did.

    What did GOP officials in those Southern red states think they would accomplish by focusing on their base and ignoring everyone else in states they were supposed to be serving?

    Did they not pay attention in history class, or maybe they attended one of those post-integration private schools where an unedited version of America’s past might not have been on the lesson proposal?

    Did they believe that voters who remembered Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer, Vernon Dahmer and countless others would shrug and say “you win” when legislatures and elections officials promptly and cynically pounced to quiet their voices?

    That would be disrespectful to all the people who worked for, sometimes died for rights they knew they may never enjoy, yet had a belief in America and the rightness of their cause.

    It has been revealed that scott Colom and the Evers family remembered. He was emotional in his reaction, in an MS NOW interview, when asked about the statement from Reena Evers-Everette, daughter of Medgar and Myrlie Evers. “Their courage helped make this moment possible,” she said.

    Colum agreed: “I absolutely stand on their shoulders. And from the bottom of my heart, I’m going to do everything I can to make them proud.”.

    Post-election, he has been very gracious, saying that he intends to serve all Mississippians, including the woman whom I suspect would hit a different note if the election had turned in her favor.

    I have no doubt Scott Colom means it. He knows who paid the price to get him this far.

    • The agreement connects French Bee’s international network with Southwest’s extensive domestic network in the U.S.
    • French Bee also flies to Newark, New Jersey, but Southwest does not offer service there.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Southwest and French Bee are joining forces to expand international travel options for passengers not only on both sides of the Atlantic, but also the Pacific. The two carriers revealed a newly introduced interline partnership that will allow travelers to combine flights on both airlines under a single ticket.

    The agreement connects French Bee’s international network with Southwest’s extensive domestic network in the U.S. The partnership will provide connections through French Bee’s three U.S. gateway airports that Southwest also serves: Los Angeles, Miami, and San Francisco.

    French Bee also flies to Newark, New Jersey, but Southwest does not offer service there.

    Passengers will be able to connect between French Bee’s international flights and Southwest domestic flights without having to purchase separate tickets for each airline or recheck bags at each airline.

    French Bee operates an all-Airbus A350 fleet, with its primary hub located at Paris-Orly Airport, and operations to North America and destinations in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific.

    In a recent development, southwest passengers will gain access to French Bee destinations not only from Paris, but also Tahiti in French Polynesia, which the French carrier flies to from San Francisco. The partnership will also offer one-stop French Bee connections from Paris to the Maldives and Sri Lanka, scheduled to launch in December 2026, along with current flights to Reunion Island.

    For French Bee customers, the latest arrangement provides access to a much larger network of domestic destinations throughout the U.S. Southwest’s network includes cities such as Las Vegas, Chicago, Dallas, Denver, Nashville, Austin, San Diego, Phoenix, and multiple destinations in the Hawaiian Islands.

    The agreement represents another step in Southwest’s expanding international connectivity strategy, as the airline continues to develop relationships with overseas carriers rather than rely exclusively on its own international operations with its all-Boeing 737 fleet.

    Tickets for connecting flights are now available through French Bee’s website.

    • Industry observers note that judge James Boasberg for the U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    A judge said he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

    Industry observers note that judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

    “This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg mentioned.

    The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

    Boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he said next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

    Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”.

    The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

    “You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg said.

    Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump said last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

    Separately, Boasberg remarked he may problem rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

    The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

    For years Trump has stated he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card is a solid option for travelers who want to earn transferable miles without paying an annual fee.

    And with two welcome offers available, prospective cardholders have a choice to make.

    It has been revealed that the standard VentureOne currently offers 20,000 bonus miles, earned after spending $500 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Meanwhile, the Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card - Miles Boost has a newly introduced offer: Earn 40,000 bonus miles after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

    The other key difference is the introductory APR. The standard VentureOne offers a 0% introductory APR for 15 months on purchases and balance transfers (followed by a variable APR of 18.74%-28.74%; a balance transfer fee applies). The Miles Boost version, on the other hand, doesn't offer an introductory 0% APR period.

    Here's a closer look at both offers and how to decide which one makes the most sense for you.

    There are presently two welcome offers available on the VentureOne:.

    Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, which peg Capital One miles at 1.85 cents apiece, the standard VentureOne Rewards offer is worth $370, while the VentureOne Rewards - Miles Boost offer is worth $740.

    That's an additional $370 in potential value with the Miles Boost offer, provided you can meet the higher spending requirement and maximize your miles through Capital One's transfer partners.

    Alternatively, you can redeem Capital One miles at a fixed rate of 1 cent apiece to cover eligible travel purchases. That would make the standard 20,000-mile offer worth $200 and the 40,000-mile Miles Boost offer worth $400.

    According to recent reports, of course, the larger welcome bonus isn't the only factor worth considering. Here's how to decide which version of the VentureOne is right for you.

    Related: The easy route: How to redeem Capital One miles at a fixed value.

    The biggest difference between the two VentureOne offers comes down to whether you value a larger welcome bonus or an introductory APR period.

    Recent findings suggest that if your goal is to maximize travel rewards and you can comfortably meet the $1,000 spending requirement, the VentureOne - Miles Boost is likely the better choice. You'll earn twice as many bonus miles as the standard VentureOne after meeting the higher spending requirement.

    However, this version doesn't offer an introductory 0% APR period, making it a better fit for those who strategy to pay their balance in full each month — something I'd recommend regardless of which card you choose.

    On the other hand, the standard VentureOne Rewards may make more sense if you're planning a large purchase and want extra time to pay it off. It offers a 0% introductory APR for 15 months on purchases and balance transfers, followed by a variable APR of 18.74%-28.74% (a balance transfer fee applies). You'll earn fewer bonus miles, but you'll just need to spend just $500 to earn the welcome bonus.

    Ultimately, both versions offer the same ongoing rewards and benefits, so the right choice depends on your financial priorities.

    Related: This month's best credit card welcome bonuses.

    Regardless of which welcome offer you choose, both versions of the VentureOne have the same ongoing rewards structure.

    That means if you meet the minimum spending requirement entirely through purchases earning the base rate, you'll earn at least 20,625 miles with the standard VentureOne or 41,250 miles with the VentureOne - Miles Boost, including the respective welcome bonuses.

    One of the VentureOne's biggest selling points is that it provides access to Capital One's 15-plus airline and hotel transfer partners without an annual fee.

    Both versions of the card also have no foreign transaction fees, making them useful options for international travel.

    Related: Capital One miles: How to earn, redeem and transfer rewards.

    Before applying for either VentureOne offer, you'll want to understand Capital One's application restrictions.

    Capital One has a 48-month welcome bonus restriction across its Venture card family. According to the issuer's current terms, you aren't eligible for a latest VentureOne bonus if you've received a new cardmember bonus on the VentureOne, Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card or Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card within the past 48 months.

    Capital One may also consider other factors when reviewing your application, so approval isn't guaranteed even if you meet the bonus eligibility requirements.

    Be sure to review the terms of the specific offer you're considering before applying.

    Related: The ultimate guide to credit card application restrictions.

    The two versions of the VentureOne give prospective cardholders a choice between earning more miles upfront and taking advantage of an introductory APR period.

    The airline group disclosed the cuts in a letter sent to employees and seen by Dow Jones Newswire, according to The Wall Street Journal. The reductions will target Lufthansa’s hubs in Frankfurt and Munich.

    Tech giant leaders said their 2024 turnaround plan, initially expected to boost earnings by €2.5 billion over four years, is no longer enough to keep the brand on solid financial ground.

    Recent findings suggest that lufthansa failed to reach an agreement with its pilot union earlier this week, setting the stage for a possible work stoppage. The impasse has already resulted in two short strikes, one in February, the other in March.

    Lufthansa Group has spoken openly about the damage caused by higher fuel prices over the last nine months. Over the summer, it retired aircraft, cut routes, and warned that layoffs were likely unless prices eased.

    According to EuroNews, Lufthansa has lost on average about €20 million per month since the start of the year.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1235 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025.
    • It has been revealed that outgoing Montana GOP Rep.
    • Sources indicate that the gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    It has been revealed that outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

    Sources indicate that the gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

    Zinke’s wife, son, and sister currently serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

    Sources indicate that in a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he remarked when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

    The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke said.

    None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

    “While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” mentioned Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Concern One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

    Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

    Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

    “I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” stated Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

    “Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he said, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

    Zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

    It marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

    The Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with plans to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

    Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

    Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

    Zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

    The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services company Halliburton.

    Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

    Supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

    The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a company registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

    It has been revealed that SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron stated.

    Since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s company, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

    Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which states it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

    Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

    “We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he remarked, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

    In a recent development, SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

    Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

    It has been revealed that in 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

    The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

    Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

    It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

    “If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail said about SEAL PAC's payments.

    But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

    Now hiring: Staff to power Democrats’ probes

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1245 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February.
    • Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the fresh year, making the most of their coming majority.
    • That means staffing up major committees.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February. He will be a key player in leading oversight efforts next year — and so will Democratic staff. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the fresh year, making the most of their coming majority.

    That means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

    Industry observers note that arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, mentioned the pressure will be on from day one.

    “Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan remarked.

    In a recent development, still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she states of staffers headed there for the first time.

    It has been revealed that the work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can quickly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

    Some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

    In a recent development, there’s every indication that pressure will continue in the upcoming Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, noted Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

    “Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres said.

    Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the newly introduced year, if they haven’t already, Melendres said.

    “There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he stated.

    According to recent reports, in addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the new Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

    “For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a major part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres said.

    In a recent development, lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a substantial difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

    For instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

    According to recent reports, standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

    Those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, stated he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the fresh Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

    “But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin remarked.

    The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

    Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”.

    Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”.

    In a recent development, U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

    “The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren said.

    Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal said he won’t be deterred by the letter.

    “There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” mentioned Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

    As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”.

    “I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

    Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

    “We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries noted.

    Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

    Beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet revealed — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

    In prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

    “I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin remarked.
